contexts.text: Implementing microservices poses challenges in service discovery due to dynamic changes in service instances and their contexts, requiring mechanisms that handle uncertainty and variability in QoS and context.
contexts.original_text: Like most transformational trends, implementing microservices poses its own challenges: Hundreds of microservices may be composed to form a complex architecture; tens of instances of the same microservice can run on different servers; the number or locations of running instances could change very frequently. Moreover, the set of service instances changes dynamically because of autoscaling, failures, and upgrades. Therefore, one of the challenges in a microservice architecture concerns how services discover, connect, and interact with each other. Consequently, elaborated service discovery mechanisms are required [19].

contexts.text: Existing service discovery solutions do not explicitly consider transient and continuously changing context and QoS profiles of services, which can affect service selection quality.
contexts.original_text: These solutions do not take explicitly into account the context and quality of services, that are transient and continuously change over time because of several different reasons – e.g., a service consumer/provider can change its context because of mobility/elasticity, a service provider can change its QoS profile according to day time, etc. In this settings, our approach envisages a new service discovery mechanism able to deal with uncertainty and potential adverse effects attributed to frequent variability of the context and QoS profile of services.

contexts.text: Ensuring that continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) models accurately represent the behavior of component-based software to support valid quality property analysis and software engineering decisions.
contexts.original_text: As such, ensuring that the analysis is accurate by using CTMCs that closely model the behaviour of the analysed software has received relatively little attention.

contexts.text: Improving the accuracy of quality property analysis of software systems modeled by CTMCs, overcoming the limitations of the exponential distribution assumption for operation execution times.
contexts.original_text: Our paper addresses this challenge for continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs), a type of stochastic state-transition models used to analyse quality software properties both at design time and at runtime.

contexts.name: Continuous-Time Markov Chains (CTMCs)
contexts.description: Mathematical models for stochastic processes evolving in time with the Markov property, used to analyze quality properties of software.
contexts.original_text: Markov chains are mathematical models for stochastic processes evolving in time. A continuous-time stochastic process X(t) with countable state space S is a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) if it has the Markov property.

contexts.name: Phase-Type Distributions (PHDs)
contexts.description: Distributions used to model variations in execution times of software components more accurately than exponential distributions in CTMCs.
contexts.original_text: OMNI comprises two stages. The first stage makes the CTMC more realistic through the addition of states and transitions that model the fact that software components have non-zero minimum execution times. We use additional states and transitions corresponding to Erlang distributions for this purpose. The CTMC is then further refined in the second OMNI stage by using phase-type distributions to model the variations in the execution time of the components.

contexts.name: OMNI Method
contexts.description: A tool-supported observation-based Markov chain refinement method that improves the accuracy of CTMC models for software quality property analysis by refining high-level CTMCs using observed execution times of components.
contexts.original_text: We introduce an observation-based Markov chain refinement (OMNI) method that significantly improves the accuracy with which quality software properties can be analysed. OMNI starts from a high-level abstract CTMC whose states correspond to operations performed by different components of the analysed system, and uses observed execution times for the components to refine this CTMC.

The first stage makes the CTMC more realistic through the addition of states and transitions that model the fact that software components have non-zero minimum execution times. We use additional states and transitions corresponding to Erlang distributions for this purpose. The CTMC is then further refined in the second OMNI stage by using phase-type distributions to model the variations in the execution time of the components.

contexts.name: Tool Implementation and Case Study
contexts.description: A tool implementing OMNI that produces refined CTMC models compatible with probabilistic model checkers like PRISM, demonstrated through a case study showing improved accuracy and avoidance of invalid design decisions.
contexts.original_text: In addition, we provide a tool that implements the OMNI method, producing refined CTMC models that can be analysed with the probabilistic model checker PRISM. Finally, we present a case study that shows how software engineers can use OMNI to avoid multiple invalid design decisions suggested by traditional CTMC analysis.

contexts.text: Existing anomaly detection methods are either absent in runtime decision-making or difficult to tailor to domain-specific needs.
contexts.original_text: However, currently, anomaly detection is either absent in runtime decision-making approaches for continuous experimentation and self-adaptation or difficult to tailor to domain-specific needs.

contexts.text: There is a need for a generic and tunable anomaly detection framework that can be adapted to different domains and incorporate expert input.
contexts.original_text: In this paper, we contribute by proposing a framework that simplifies the detection of data anomalies in timeseries-outputs of running systems. contexts.name: Two-Stage Anomaly Detection Method
contexts.description: A semi-automated method that identifies strong seasonal patterns and critical anomaly thresholds, allowing automated anomaly detection after an initial learning phase with expert input.
contexts.original_text: Concretely, anomaly detection should consider the running experiments and their expected effect, e.g. whether they change the model of normal behavior of a timeseries. At the same time, the experimentation engine should be aware of the expected anomalies (e.g. due to external circumstances such as holidays) in the timeseries of a system metric. In response, in this paper we provide a simple yet robust way to detect anomalies in arbitrary timeseries and connect anomaly detection to experimentation and self-adaptation. Our method works in two stages: identification of strong seasonal patterns and identification of critical anomaly thresholds. It is a semi-automated method in the sense that, although it assumes the involvement of domain experts in the learning phase, it can work in a completely automated way after that.

contexts.text: Architecture Smells (ASs) are design decisions that negatively affect system quality attributes such as reusability and testability, but receive less attention than code smells in research and practice.
contexts.original_text: Architecture Smells (ASs) are design decisions that can have significant negative effects on a systems quality attributes such as reusability and testability. ASs are focused on higher level of software systems than code smells, which are implementation-level constructs. ASs can have much wider impact on a system than code smells. However, ASs usually receive less attention than code smells in both research and practice.

contexts.text: There is a lack of empirical studies focusing on practitioners' perception of ASs and how they detect and refactor ASs.
contexts.original_text: Despite that researchers proposed a catalogue of ASs and corresponding architectural refactorings 8 , it is not clear how well their definitions of ASs are accepted and to what extent their refactoring approaches and tools are adopted by practitioners when detecting and refactoring ASs. There is a lack of empirical studies focusing on practitioners perception of ASs and how they detect and refactor ASs.

contexts.name: Exploratory Study on Developers' Perception of Architecture Smells
contexts.description: Conducted an exploratory study analyzing 207 Stack Overflow posts using Grounded Theory to understand how developers describe, cause, detect, refactor, and perceive the impact and challenges of Architecture Smells.
contexts.original_text: We have conducted an exploratory study of developers conception of ASs by analyzing related discussions in Stack Overflow. We used 14 ASs related terms to search the relevant posts in Stack Overflow and extracted 207 posts. We used Grounded Theory method for analyzing the extracted posts about developers description of ASs, causes of ASs, approaches and tools for detecting and refactoring ASs, quality attributes affected by ASs, and difficulties in detecting and refactoring ASs.

contexts.name: Identification of Key Findings on Architecture Smells
contexts.description: Found that developers often use general terms to describe ASs; ASs are mainly caused by violating architecture patterns, design principles, or misusing architecture antipatterns; there is a lack of dedicated tools for detecting and refactoring ASs; maintainability and performance are main concerns; and challenges include inability to quantify cost-benefit and lack of approaches and tools.
contexts.original_text: Our findings show that: (1) developers often describe ASs with some general terms; (2) ASs are mainly caused by violating architecture patterns, design principles, or misusing architecture antipatterns; (3) there is a lack of dedicated tools for detecting and refactoring ASs; (4) developers mainly concern about the maintainability and performance of systems affected by ASs; and (5) the inability to quantify the cost and benefit as well as the lack of approaches and tools makes detecting and refactoring ASs difficult.

contexts.original_text: Our findings show that: (1) developers often describe ASs with some general terms; (2) ASs are mainly caused by violating architecture patterns, design principles, or misusing architecture antipatterns; (3) there is a lack of dedicated tools for detecting and refactoring ASs; (4) developers mainly concern about the maintainability and performance of systems affected by ASs; and (5) the inability to quantify the cost and benefit as well as the lack of approaches and tools makes detecting and refactoring ASs difficult.

contexts.text: Cyber-physical systems are vulnerable to information leaks, and software architects need to reason about security policies to define desired and undesired information flow through a system, especially when using microservice architectures that require refinement of macro-level policies into micro-level policies for individual microservices.
contexts.original_text: Since cyber-physical systems are inherently vulnera- ble to information leaks, software architects need to reason about security policies to define desired and undesired information flow through a system. The microservice architectural style requires the architects to refine a macro-level security policy into micro-level policies for individual microservices.

contexts.text: Ill-formed refinement of security policies in microservice compositions can lead to information leaks, and existing approaches do not adequately consider cyber-physical system characteristics like real-time behavior or asynchronous message passing communication.
contexts.original_text: However, when policies are refined in an ill-formed way, information leaks can emerge on composition of microservices. Related approaches to prevent such leaks do not take into account characteristics of cyber-physical systems like real-time behavior or message passing communication.

contexts.text: Information flow security is not generally compositional, so even if local security policies are satisfied, their composition can introduce global information leaks, which is a challenge in microservice architectures with finer-grained policies.
contexts.original_text: Using these lo- cal policies to reason about the overall system security requires compositionality of the verification. Unfortunately, it is a well- known fact that information flow security is not generally compositional. Thus, even if all local security policies are satisfied, composing them in an ill-formed way can introduce global information leaks.

contexts.text: Existing architectural security approaches lack formal rigor of information flow or do not consider cyber-physical system characteristics such as real-time constraints, asynchronous communication, and feedback composition.
contexts.original_text: Related work on architectural security either lacks the for- mal rigor of information flow, or does not take a num- ber of cyber-physical system characteristics into account. Namely, these systems must satisfy real-time constraints imposed by their environment. The resulting time-dependent behavior must be considered during the verification to detect implicit information leaks that are exploitable by observing the systems response times. Also, existing approaches assume a synchronous handshake communication between components. In contrast, cyber-physical systems interact asynchronously by lightweight message passing. Finally, cyber-physical systems implement complex, application-level interaction protocols that are based on a two-way communication. This so-called feedback is known as the most restrictive form of composition that often prevents a compositional verification.

contexts.text: Evaluating the accuracy of a compositional verification approach for microservice security policies using the CoCoME case study, comparing verification results of microservices against expected security outcomes to identify secure and insecure architectures.
contexts.original_text: To analyse the outcomes of our study, we compare the results obtained from the verification against the expected security results. Thereby, we check if our predefined expectations are satisfied. If the system is expected to be secure with respect to a policy, that expectation is satisfied if all the microservices are also verified as secure. In contrast, an insecure expectation is satisfied if at least one of the microservices is insecure according to the verification.

contexts.text: Challenges in verifying microservice security policies include memory limitations of verification tools and abstraction from explicit data handling, which may mask false positives or negatives.
contexts.original_text: In case of the Application, no results are available for two policies due to excess memory usage of UPPAAL. ... our implementations omit the explicit data handling of microservices. Thus, we abstract from the way that individual parameters are processed, stored, and propagated. Thereby, we might have masked both false positive and false negative errors.

contexts.text: Limitations in generalizing findings from the CoCoME case study to cyber-physical systems with hard real-time constraints and physical hardware interactions.
contexts.original_text: In particular, no hard real-time constraints are imposed on the system by the physical environment. Therefore, our findings might not be generalizable to cases that actually show these characteristics.

contexts.name: Information Flow Security
contexts.description: A theory that analyzes system behavior with respect to information leaks by classifying information into secret, public, and neutral levels, and ensuring that secret information does not influence public information observable by third parties.
contexts.original_text: The theory of information flow security allows to analyze the behavior of a system with respect to information leaks. Intuitively, a system is secure if secrets are never made public. Thus, secret information processed by a system must not be deducible through the public information that the system ex- changes with untrusted third parties. To that end, the approach considers information at different levels of sensitivity: secret information must not be disclosed to the public. Therefore, the behavior of a system must not allow third parties to deduce which secret information is processed. public information is exchanged with third parties. Thus, the system behavior must ensure that observing this information does not enable any deductions about secrets. neutral information is neither secret nor public. In con- trast to secret information, it may be disclosed to third parties. In contrast to public information, observing neu- tral information may enable deductions about secrets.

contexts.name: Perturbation Correction
contexts.description: A concept in information flow security where changes in secret information (perturbations) must not influence public information, but may influence neutral information which can be used for correction to keep public information uninfluenced.
contexts.original_text: Information flow security requires the behavior of a system to prevent secret information from influencing public information. In order to define the meaning of influence more precisely, the approach relies on the notion of perturbation. A perturbation is a change in the amount of the secret information that a system processes during an execution. Perturbing secret information must have no influence on the public information processed during that execution, otherwise an information flow from secret to public would be possible. Perturbations of secret information may, however, influence neutral information. This is an important factor as it allows for a correction in response to a pertur- bation. By means of a correction, a system adjusts the amount of neutral information processed during an execution, thereby allowing the public information to remain uninfluenced.

contexts.name: Generalized Noninterference
contexts.description: An information flow security property that restricts perturbations to inputs and allows corrections via neutral inputs or outputs, preserved under asynchronous feedback composition.
contexts.original_text: Our approach is based on generalized noninterference, a traditional information flow property that restricts perturbations to inputs. Hence, to perturb a system, secret inputs are both added to or deleted from the execution. In response to the perturbation, the system may add or delete neutral inputs or outputs to produce a corrected execution without influencing any public information. Generalized noninterference is known to be preserved on feedback composition, provided that the underlying communication between the composed subsystems is asynchronous.

contexts.name: Simulation Preorder
contexts.description: A behavioral relation used as a verification technique where the original system must simulate all public observations allowed by a perturbed variant to ensure public information is uninfluenced by secrets.
contexts.original_text: Since public information needs to be uninfluenced by secrets, the public observations allowed by a system must subsume all the public observations allowed by a perturbed variant of the same system. In the scope of state transition systems, such a behavioral relation is expressible in terms of a simulation preorder. Thus, the original system must be able to simulate all the public observations allowed by the perturbed variant. In this paper, we use simulations as our underlying verification technique.

contexts.text: Engineering IoT systems is challenging due to dynamicity and uncertainty of the environment, including human involvement, and the need for systems to cope with dynamic changes and deployment issues.
contexts.original_text: Engineering Internet of Things (IoT) systems is a challenging task partly due to the dynamicity and uncertainty of the environment including the involvement of the human in the loop. Users should be able to achieve their goals seamlessly in different environments, and IoT systems should be able to cope with dynamic changes. Several approaches have been proposed to enable the automated formation, enactment, and self-adaptation of goal-driven IoT systems. However, they do not address deployment issues.

contexts.text: Existing approaches for dynamic formation and adaptation of goal-driven IoT systems do not address deployment issues such as automated placement of functionalities within hardware infrastructure and self-adaptation to changes in deployment topologies.
contexts.original_text: Several approaches have been proposed to enable the dynamic formation, enactment, and self-adaptation of GDS. However, they do not address deployment issues, such as the automated placement of the GDS functionalities within a hardware infrastructure. Additionally, among the works that focus on the deployment of IoT systems, very few aim at enabling the systems to self-adapt to dynamic changes in their deployment topologies, such as, the sudden unavailability of the deployment nodes and the degradation of the quality of their services or interconnections.

contexts.text: Deployment of goal-driven IoT systems is complex due to variability in the number and types of devices, heterogeneous hardware infrastructures, different performance requirements, and sudden changes in system constituents or deployment topologies.
contexts.original_text: The deployment of GDS is a complex process partly due to the following reasons. The number and types of the things that constitute a GDS formed to achieve a goal can be different from an environment to another based on the available devices. Moreover, the dynamically formed GDS may have different performance requirements based on the requested goals. Additionally, the hardware infrastructures in different environments are heterogeneous with respect to their processing and storage capabilities and interconnections. Furthermore, changes in the status of the systems constituents and or the deployment topologies can happen suddenly.

contexts.name: Goal-Driven IoT System (GDS)
contexts.description: A system composed of devices with individual functionalities that connect and cooperate temporarily to achieve user goals, dynamically formed based on available devices and goals.
contexts.original_text: A Goal-Driven IoT System (GDS) is composed of a set of devices with individual functionalities that connect and cooperate temporally to achieve the user goal. In previous studies, we referred to GDS as Emergent Configurations. For instance, a GDS could be dynamically formed by connecting a light sensor and two connected lamps to achieve the goal adjust the light level in a smart meeting room.

contexts.name: Deployment Models for IoT Systems
contexts.description: Models include Everything in the Cloud, Everything in the Edge, and Hybrid Edge-Cloud, each with different properties in terms of response time, availability, privacy, and quality characteristics.
contexts.original_text: In general, IoT systems can be deployed according to the following models: 1) Everything in the Cloud model: In this model, the software components of IoT systems are placed in the Cloud. It is suitable when the systems require significant elastic processing and storage capabilities or when their constituents are scattered in various areas. 2) Everything in the Edge model: The software components of IoT systems are placed in networks of more constrained devices with respect to the Cloud (e.g., local servers and gateways) that are at the Edge of the network. In this model, the computational capabilities are lower than those within the Cloud-based model. 3) Hybrid Edge-Cloud model: The software components of IoT systems are distributed across the Cloud and the Edge of the network. Thus, it enables exploiting the advantages of the other two models. For instance, it supports deploying the components that should perform processes with low latency in the Edge of the network, and deploying those that perform resource-demanding processes in the Cloud. These deployment models have different properties in terms of response time, availability, privacy, and other quality characteristics.

contexts.name: Deployment Models for IoT Systems
contexts.description: Models include Everything in the Cloud, Everything in the Edge, and Hybrid Edge-Cloud, each with different properties in terms of response time, availability, privacy, and quality characteristics.
contexts.original_text: In general, IoT systems can be deployed according to the following models: 1) Everything in the Cloud model: In this model, the software components of IoT systems are placed in the Cloud. It is suitable when the systems require significant elastic processing and storage capabilities or when their constituents are scattered in various areas. 2) Everything in the Edge model: The software components of IoT systems are placed in networks of more constrained devices with respect to the Cloud (e.g., local servers and gateways) that are at the Edge of the network. In this model, the computational capabilities are lower than those within the Cloud-based model. 3) Hybrid Edge-Cloud model: The software components of IoT systems are distributed across the Cloud and the Edge of the network. Thus, it enables exploiting the advantages of the other two models. For instance, it supports deploying the components that should perform processes with low latency in the Edge of the network, and deploying those that perform resource-demanding processes in the Cloud. These deployment models have different properties in terms of response time, availability, privacy, and other quality characteristics.

contexts.text: The paper addresses the limitation of existing probabilistic model synthesis methods that assume system parameters match exactly those of the model, which is unrealistic and limits robustness.
contexts.original_text: However, these promising approaches unrealistically assume that the parameters of the real system (e.g. service rates) will accurately match the parameters of the repaired or synthesised model. This assumption limits the usefulness of existing model repair and synthesis solutions, as Markov models are typically nonlinear, so slight differences between the actual and assumed parameters can lead to major differences between the real and modelled quality attributes of software systems.

contexts.text: It is difficult for software architects to focus their attention effectively given their broad responsibilities across technical aspects of projects.
contexts.original_text: In our research and practice in the field of software architecture, we have noticed and experienced that it is difficult for software architects to focus their attention. The software architect’s responsibilities are broad and in principle they can be involved in almost any technical aspect of a project from requirements to operational concerns.

contexts.text: Understanding how successful software architects focus their attention and whether common role-specific heuristics exist that can be taught to new architects.
contexts.original_text: However, we also observe that successful software architects appear to be very good at focusing their attention effectively, which led us to wonder how they achieve this. They may use time management techniques (like [2]) but we wondered whether there are common role-specific heuristics which could be taught to new architects.

contexts.name: Risk-Driven Architecture
contexts.description: An architectural method that prioritizes architectural decisions based on risk and cost to guide architects on where to focus their attention.
contexts.original_text: When we started investigating this topic, we were primarily interested in how practitioners really worked. However, we also performed a literature search to find related work from the research community. We did not find any studies investigating the specific topic we are interested in, but an architectural method which helps architects to focus their attention is Risk and Cost Driven Architecture (RCDA) [11]. This method transforms the architect’s approach from defining architectural structures early in a project, to providing a stream of decisions throughout it, prioritising their work using the risk and cost of open decisions.

contexts.text: Are there common heuristics which experienced architects use to focus their attention?
contexts.original_text: In a previous study [15], we decided to investigate this via a questionnaire-based study of a group of experienced architects. We discovered that there are common heuristics which experienced architects use to focus their attention and we created a model to capture and relate them.

contexts.text: How can the model of heuristics for focusing architectural attention be validated and refined with a wider group of software and enterprise architects?
contexts.original_text: In this paper we explain how, in a second study, we then validated the model with a much wider group of software and enterprise architects, via an online questionnaire, and refined the model based on their input.

contexts.name: Validated Model of Heuristics for Focusing Architectural Attention
contexts.description: A simple, coherent model capturing common heuristics used by experienced software architects to focus their attention effectively, validated with a broad group of practitioners.
contexts.original_text: The contribution of our work is not the heuristics in our model, as most of them are quite familiar to experienced practitioners. Our contribution is to capture them clearly in a simple, coherent model, and to validate their value to experienced practitioners. Our work makes the implicit knowledge held in the heads of experienced architects explicit and accessible.

contexts.text: Updating air-gapped service-based software systems in mission-critical settings poses challenges including ensuring verifiably correct update configurations, managing containerized services with different runtime environments, and recording update actions for auditability and regulatory compliance.
contexts.original_text: However, updating air-gapped systems raises several issues from a software architecture perspective, especially given the overall mission-critical setting; those include: (i) the configuration of components produced to update the system should be verifiably correct, since there is significant cost-to-repair for incorrect updates, (ii) service-based architectures entail containerized services, with support of different runtime environments, and (iii) update actions should be recorded in a traceable manner, in order to support auditability and regulatory compliance.

contexts.name: Semantic Versioning
contexts.description: A versioning scheme using three numbers (major.minor.patch) to indicate breaking changes, backward-compatible functionality additions, and bug fixes respectively.
contexts.original_text: For our service-based setting, we adopt semantic versioning [13], where three numbers separated by a dot are used, e.g. “2.4.1.” The first number indicates a major release typically introducing breaking changes. The middle number reflects a minor version change, signalling that new functionality has been added but with full backwards compatibility preserved. The last number stands for patch or micro changes which indicates bug fixes; patch changes are also fully backwards compatible.

contexts.text: The paper addresses the problem of understanding why implementations of continuous integration in large-scale industry projects differ from the ideal practices described in literature, and what impediments must be overcome to enable more frequent software delivery to the mainline.
contexts.original_text: But the question still remains why the implementations of continuous integration in industry projects differ so much from the practice as it is described in literature, for example in Martin Fowlers popular paper 3 . We have, as one small step to answer this question, in previous work reported our own experiences of factors that could constrain a full implementation of continuous integration 8 . The topic of this paper is to answer the following research question: Which are the impediments that have to be overcome in order to make software developers deliver more frequently?

contexts.original_text: Continuous integration is often described as an efficient way of conducting software development. The practice and its benefits are described in both books and other research papers 2,5,12,14 . Still, many projects struggle to realize their implementations of continuous integration 10,13,15,16 .

contexts.name: Large-scale software-intensive embedded systems
contexts.description: Complex software systems integrated with electronic and mechanical components, developed by large teams often numbering in the hundreds or thousands of developers.
contexts.original_text: The topic of this paper is to answer the following research question: Which are the impediments that have to be overcome in order to make software developers deliver more frequently? We will focus on continuous integration implementations for software-intensive embedded systems (software systems combined with electronic and mechanical systems).

contexts.name: Informal Decision Making
contexts.description: Most architecture decisions are made and communicated informally, often through slide decks, wikis, and meeting recordings.
contexts.original_text: In a survey by Dasanayake, Markkula, Aaramaa and Oivo [11], architects reported that 90% of their decisions were made and communicated informally. And while these architects were mostly satisfied with their informal decision-making processes, they also recognized some challenges with revisiting design rationale, communicating decisions to customers, and in knowledge gaps between engineers and architects. In our research we also found that decisions were communicated informally through a number of media, including slide decks, wikis, and meeting recordings.

contexts.name: Kruchten's Taxonomy of Architecture Decisions
contexts.description: A classification of architecture decisions into existence decisions, bans, property decisions, and executive decisions.
contexts.original_text: Kruchten [12] proposes the following taxonomy for architecture decisions: Existence decisions state that some element or artifact will show up in the systems design or implementation. Bans or non-existence decisions are statements of things to not do. Kruchten [12] suggests that it is especially important to precisely document bans because there isnt a place for them in conventional architecture documentation. Property decisions affect the overall qualities of the system and may be represented by design rules or constraints. Executive decisions are driven by the business environment and may affect the development process or choices of technology and tools.

contexts.name: Levels of Architecture Decisions
contexts.description: Architecture decisions can be classified by levels: management (organization-level), project, architecture, and implementation levels, each with different decision makers and impacts.
contexts.original_text: While Miesbauer and Weinreich [13] found that architecture decisions could be mapped to Kruchtens taxonomy [12], they noted that architects themselves talk about decisions they make according to level. They proposed classifying architecture decisions according to these levels: Management typically makes organization-level decisions with advice from software architects. Once made these decisions are rarely revisited. Project managers, architects, and customers tend to make project-level decisions at the beginning of a project. Software architects or team leads typically make architecture-level decisions after discussion in a group. Finally, implementation-level decisions are made independently by developers and typically not documented.

contexts.name: Case Study on Architecture Decision-Making
contexts.description: A case study of a large global technology organization examining architecture decision-making approaches, challenges, context, and impact using a survey and focus groups.
contexts.original_text: This paper presents a case study of a large technology organization with multiple business units and product lines. This study examines approaches to architecture decision-making and seeks to understand in more depth the reasons for the decision-making approaches employed by architects, as well as the challenges and context that architects must deal with. In addition, this study attempts to understand the impact of architecture decisions.

contexts.name: Characterization of Architecture Decisions Beyond Existing Taxonomies
contexts.description: The study found difficulty classifying decisions using existing taxonomies and characterized decisions as technology, design guidelines, infrastructure, or product implementation level decisions, noting different impacts and perceptions.
contexts.original_text: The researchers found it difficult to classify these decisions according Miesbauer and Weinreich [13] levels or to line them up with Kruchtens taxonomy [13]. Consequently, we characterized decisions as being technology, design guidelines, infrastructure, or product implementation level decisions. Analysis revealed that technology, design guidelines, and infrastructure decisions were viewed positively, while product implementation decisions were not.

contexts.name: Insights into Informal and Political Nature of Architecture Decision-Making
contexts.description: Architects mostly use informal decision-making processes that can be political, involving persuasion, interpersonal relationships, and veto power, with some decisions made by product management without architect consultation.
contexts.original_text: Architects described their decision making as mostly informal, e.g. the right people get in a room or on a phone call and discuss. While decision-making can be informal, it can also be political. One respondent in FG1 recounted a situation where those who dissented were removed from further discussion. Another observed that conversations, and persuasion and interpersonal relationships often drive decisions, and that this was not always positive. Depending on the decision, certain people had veto power, and for some decisions, it was agreed that product management rightfully should make them, although architects would like to be consulted.

contexts.text: Architectural assumptions (AA) are important but not well managed, leading to problems such as misunderstandings and risks in software development.
contexts.original_text: AA that are not well managed (and thus remain implicit AA or become invalid AA) can lead to a multitude of problems in software development [5]. As an example of such a problem, consider architectural misunderstanding: stakeholders may misunderstand an architectural design decision, because they are not aware of the AA behind this decision. Another example is undetected risks: one essential characteristic of assumptions is uncertainty, which may lead to risks in projects, especially if AA remain implicit.

contexts.text: There is little empirical research on the notion of AA and their management in industry.
contexts.original_text: Little empirical research has been conducted regarding the notion of AA as well as their management.

contexts.text: There is a lack of approaches, tools, and guidelines for AA management, and challenges exist in managing AA.
contexts.original_text: there is a lack of approaches, tools, and guidelines for AA management, and there are certain challenges in managing AA.

contexts.text: There are several challenges in managing AA in software development, including lack of data, integration issues, and project context challenges.
contexts.original_text: Furthermore, besides the lack of guidelines, approaches, tools, resources, etc. for AA management, which have also been discussed in our survey on AA [5], we found several other challenges of AA management in software development, including “Lack of data”, “Integration”, and “Project context” as elaborated in Table 3. For example, as mentioned by the subjects, there is a lack of data (e.g., empirical data) regarding AA and their management in existing projects. This is potentially because stakeholders do not make AA explicit and document them in a systematic way. The lack of existing data regarding AA from projects is also a reason that impedes conducting individual AA management activities in software development.

contexts.name: Architectural Assumptions (AA)
contexts.description: Architectural knowledge taken for granted or accepted as true without evidence, characterized by uncertainty regarding correctness, impact, importance, and suitability.
contexts.original_text: Architectural assumptions (AAFootnote 1) are an important type of architectural knowledge in both architecting and software development in general [5]. Similar to the definition of “assumption” in Oxford English DictionaryFootnote 2 and Merriam-WebsterFootnote 3, we define AA as: architectural knowledge taken for granted, or accepted as true without evidence. The essence of the AA concept is “uncertainty”: stakeholders are not (completely) certain regarding various aspects of architectural knowledge, including correctness, impact, importance, suitability, etc.

contexts.name: Exploratory Case Study on AA and Their Management
contexts.description: Conducted an exploratory case study with 24 architects to analyze architectural assumptions and their management in industry, confirming previous survey findings and identifying new insights.
contexts.original_text: In this paper, we conducted an exploratory case study with twenty-four architects to analyze AA and their management in industry. The results confirm certain findings from our previous survey on AA [5]: (1) neither the term nor the concept of AA is commonly used in industry, and stakeholders may have different understandings of the AA concept; (2) AA are not only important in architecting, but also of paramount importance in software development as they span the whole software development lifecycle; (3) there is a lack of approaches, tools, and guidelines for AA management, and there are certain challenges in managing AA. Furthermore, we got five new findings: (1) architects frequently make AA in their work; (2) the AA concept is subjective; (3) AA are context-dependent and have a dynamic nature (e.g., turning out to be invalid or vice versa during their lifecycle); (4) there is a connection between AA and certain types of software artifacts (e.g., requirements and design decisions); (5) twelve AA management activities and four benefits of managing AA were identified.

contexts.text: Ensuring consistency between system design and adaptive as well as evolutionary changes in software artifacts to maintain accurate architectural models for performance prediction.
contexts.original_text: If models are involved in the development process and used for performance prediction, there are delays due to emerging inconsistencies between different software artifacts. The elimination of these inconsistencies is a time consuming, complex and error prone activity.

contexts.text: Limited scope of existing automated consistency preservation approaches in terms of supported change scenarios.
contexts.original_text: Currently, there are already approaches for automated consistency preservation of software artifacts. Nevertheless, the limited scope in terms of supported change scenarios is a significant disadvantage.

contexts.text: Need for continuous assessment and validation of the quality of consistency preservation in architectural models.
contexts.original_text: Ultimately, several validation steps were integrated into the approach, enabling continuous assessment regarding the quality of the consistency preservation.

contexts.text: Challenges in maintaining up-to-date and accurate architectural models during software evolution and adaptation, especially under short development cycles and high dynamics.
contexts.original_text: While software systems are becoming increasingly more complex, development cycles get shorter and shorter due to the growing popularity of practices such as DevOps. This is problematic, because due to high dynamics in terms of changes to the requirements and the infrastructure, there is the risk that the implemented application (source code) continuously drifts away from the software design (architecture). In particular, this drift is driven by software evolution and adaptation.

contexts.text: High effort and complexity in modeling and maintaining accurate software architecture models during development and operation.
contexts.original_text: The improved planning possibilities are a major advantage of the models, but a significant drawback is that the modeling process is time-consuming and challenging (P2). Furthermore, it is important that accurate models are available at any time, i.e. during evolution, but also throughout adaptations while the system is in operation (P3).

contexts.text: Delays due to inconsistencies between software artifacts during development and operation cause time-consuming, complex, and error-prone activities.
contexts.original_text: If models are involved in the development process and used for performance prediction, there are delays due to emerging inconsistencies between different software artifacts. The elimination of these inconsistencies is a time consuming, complex and error prone activity.

contexts.text: Existing automated consistency preservation approaches have limited scope in supported change scenarios, especially lacking system composition consideration and automated quality analysis.
contexts.original_text: Currently, there are already approaches for automated consistency preservation of software artifacts. Nevertheless, the limited scope in terms of supported change scenarios is a significant disadvantage. ... all three categories of approaches suffer from gaps in the extent of the consistency preservation; so far, the system composition has not yet been considered. Furthermore, automated analyses of the quality of the derived models have not been addressed at all or only in prototypical fashion.

contexts.text: Need for accurate, up-to-date architectural models during software evolution and adaptation to assess impact of design decisions and quality characteristics like performance.
contexts.original_text: Furthermore, it is important that accurate models are available at any time, i.e. during evolution, but also throughout adaptations while the system is in operation (P3). ... It is necessary to ensure consistency between the system design and adaptive as well as evolutionary changes. Otherwise, it is challenging to assess the impact of design decisions. This is important, because quality characteristics like performance heavily depend on architectural design decisions.

contexts.text: Monitoring overhead can negatively affect software performance, so monitoring granularity needs to be controlled to reduce overhead.
contexts.original_text: In order to keep the models up to date during operation, it is necessary to observe the application, for example with the help of monitoring techniques. A key disadvantage of monitoring is the introduced overhead by the measurements, which can negatively affect the performance of the observed software (P4).

contexts.text: Uncertainty in model quality leads to lack of trust in predictions based on models, requiring validation and feedback mechanisms.
contexts.original_text: A general disadvantage of using models is the fact that their quality is uncertain. In other words, there is no trust in the predictions made on the basis of the model. One must rely on the model to represent the real application well (P5).

contexts.name: Palladio Component Model (PCM)
contexts.description: A model-based approach for the analysis of software architectures focusing on performance aspects, dividing software architecture specification into five meta-models: Repository Model, System Model, Resource Environment Model, Allocation Model, and Usage Model.
contexts.original_text: The Palladio Component Model (PCM) is a model-based approach for the analysis of software architectures 31 . The PCM focuses on the evaluation of performance aspects, such as the detection of bottlenecks and scalability problems. The PCM makes it possible to make statements about the impact of design decisions at an early stage of development. As a result, high costs for wrong decisions in development can be avoided and scalable software can be designed. The PCM divides the specification of the software architecture into five different meta-models. The Repository Model contains a repository with components and interfaces. In addition, it includes the descriptions of the behavior of services that are provided by these components. These are called Service Effect Specifications (SEFFs). The System Model describes the composition of the software architecture, based on the components and interfaces specified in the repository. The Resource Environment Model reflects the actual hardware environment which is composed of containers with processing resources (e.g., CPU) and links between them. The mapping from the system composition (System Model) to the resources (Resource Environment Model) is described by the Allocation Model. Finally, the Usage Model defines the behavior of users, i.e. the way in which they interact with the system.

contexts.name: iObserve
contexts.description: An approach that uses Ops-time observations to detect changes during operation and update an architecture model for quality predictions, using PCM as basis and Kieker for monitoring.
contexts.original_text: iObserve considers the adaptation and evolution of cloud-based systems as two interwoven processes 9 . The main idea is to use Ops-time observations to detect changes during the operation and to reflect them by updating an architecture model which is then applied for quality predictions. The PCM is used as the basis for the quality predictions and Kieker is used for monitoring the system during operation 13, 9 . Briefly summarized, iObserve collects monitoring data at Ops-time with the help of Kieker and applies necessary changes to the architecture model (PCM instance) which originated at Dev-time. Adaptation and evolution are interwoven and shared models are used throughout the application life-cycle to close the gap between Ops-time and Dev-time.

contexts.name: Continuous Integration of Performance Models (CIPM)
contexts.description: An approach to update architectural models after each source code commit at Dev-time and after changes at Ops-time, integrating incremental extraction, calibration, and self-validation processes to maintain up-to-date models for performance prediction.
contexts.original_text: Continuous Integration of Performance Models CIPM (Continuous Integration of Performance Models) 25, 26 aims to update the architectural model after each source code commit at Dev-time and after changes at Ops-time. To accomplish this, CIPM extends the rule-based incremental extraction of the architecture models from Langhammer 22 with further functionalities like the incremental calibration. Furthermore, it integrates parts of iObserve to update the PMs according to Ops-time changes, i.e., changes in usage or deployment. The incremental calibration of CIPM estimates resource demands and recognizes parametric dependencies. The findings are used to update the Repository Model. For the calibration, CIPM uses an adaptive monitoring to collect the required data while the application is running. Thereby, not only information about service calls is collected (so called coarse-grained monitoring), but also about the behavior within the service calls (fine-grained monitoring) is tracked 26 . It is called adaptive, because just the parts that have been changed are instrumented fine granular. Besides, the fine-grained monitoring can be deactivated to reduce the monitoring overhead. To control which services have to be observed fine granular, CIPM proposes the so-called Instrumentation Model, which stores instrumentation points and their status. After the calibration of the architecture model, CIPM starts a self-validation process. It simulates the calibrated model and compares the simulation results to the monitoring data. Recognized deviations can then be used to adjust the monitoring and calibration process in order to eliminate them.

contexts.name: Service-Call-Graph (SCG)
contexts.description: A data structure representing the system composition by capturing service call relationships between components, extracted at Dev-time from source code with developer support and at Ops-time from monitoring data including host information.
contexts.original_text: With the help of a newly introduced data structure, the so-called Service-Call-Graph (SCG), the system composition in the architecture model can now be updated in an automated way.

contexts.name: Validation Feedback Loop (VFL)
contexts.description: A mechanism that continuously evaluates the accuracy of performance predictions by comparing simulation results of models with monitoring data, enabling dynamic intervention and adjustment of monitoring granularity to improve model accuracy and reduce overhead.
contexts.original_text: An important innovation of our approach is the so-called Validation Feedback Loop (VFL). The idea is to continuously evaluate the accuracy of the performance predictions related to the derived models. In order to determine the prediction accuracy of a model, it is necessary to have a baseline. We use measurements from the real system as reference, which are available in the form of monitoring data. By comparing simulation data of the models with the monitoring data, it can be assessed how well the models represent the actually observed system in its current state. In case of high deviations, it is possible to intervene.

contexts.name: Transformation Pipeline
contexts.description: A pipeline at Ops-time that processes monitoring data to update a PCM instance, consisting of several transformations including preprocessing, resource environment update, system composition update, calibration, and finalization with validation and monitoring granularity adjustment.
contexts.original_text: The core at Ops-time is a transformation pipeline that processes the monitoring data with the goal of updating a PCM instance (similar to iObserve 9 ). In order to realize the transformation pipeline we used a tee and join pipeline architecture 6 , based on parts of iObserve 9 and the CIPM approach 25 . Fig. 4 shows the structure of the entire transformation pipeline.

contexts.name: Comprehensive approach for automated consistency preservation between system design and adaptive as well as evolutionary changes covering both Dev-time and Ops-time.
contexts.description: The approach extends existing methods by including system composition analysis and automated updates using a Service-Call-Graph (SCG), enabling an up-to-date architecture model for performance predictions at any time.
contexts.original_text: The main contributions of our approach are: (i) In-depth automated consistency preservation between system design and adaptive as well as evolutionary changes. By covering both Dev-time and Ops-time, an architecture model is available at any point in time and can be used for performance predictions (P3). In comparison to existing approaches, the system composition is included in the process. It is analyzed at Dev-time based on the source code and at Ops-time based on monitoring events. With the help of a newly introduced data structure, the so-called Service-Call-Graph (SCG), the system composition in the architecture model can now be updated in an automated way. All in all, the modeling effort can be reduced (P2) and with the help of accurate models, architecture decisions can be evaluated in a profound way (P1). Sec. V describes this enhancement in more detail.

contexts.name: Extension of self-validation with a Validation Feedback Loop (VFL) to dynamically react to recognized inaccuracies in the models.
contexts.description: The approach increases the scope of self-validations and integrates feedback from validation results into the consistency preservation process, enabling the system to learn from previous shortcomings and improve model accuracy.
contexts.original_text: (ii) Extension of the self-validations, based on the CIPM approach. The scope of self-validations is increased, recognized inaccuracies are passed into the consistency preservation process, which allows the process to react to them (P5). As a result, the maintenance of consistency relationships becomes more dynamic and can learn from previous shortcomings. The component of our approach that realizes this strategy is called Validation Feedback Loop (VFL) and is introduced in Sec. VI.

contexts.name: Design and implementation of a transformation pipeline that updates the architecture model at Ops-time using monitoring events and adjusts monitoring granularity based on validation results.
contexts.description: This pipeline enables dynamic adjustment of monitoring detail to reduce overhead while maintaining model accuracy, by increasing granularity when inaccuracies are detected and reducing it when the model is sufficiently accurate.
contexts.original_text: (iii) Design and implementation of a transformation pipeline that uses monitoring events as input to update the architecture model at Ops-time. Based on the validation results, the monitoring is adjusted at Ops-time. In case of large inaccuracies, the level of detail of the monitoring, denoted as granularity, can be increased. On the other hand, the monitoring granularity can be reduced if the model is accurate enough. As a result, the arising overhead can be reduced (P4). Sec. VII provides an overview of the pipeline structure.

contexts.text: The paper addresses the problem of extracting and classifying architectural design decisions (ADDs) that are not systematically documented in architectural knowledge management (AKM) tools but are implicitly captured in issue management systems.

contexts.name: Issue Management Systems
contexts.description: Systems like JIRA and GitHub issue tracker used to manage tasks, features, bugs, and implicitly capture design decisions through issue tracking and linking to source code commits.
contexts.original_text: The use of issue management systems (for example, JIRA and GitHub issue tracker) for managing issues is becoming popular both in industrial settings as well as in OSS projects [2, 12]. An issue is either a task, new feature, user story, or bug. These systems provide a common interface for stakeholders to track, communicate, and visualize the progress of tasks within a project.

contexts.name: ADD Categories by Kruchten
contexts.description: An ontology classifying architectural design decisions into existence decisions, property decisions, and executive decisions, with existence decisions further divided into structural, behavioral, and ban decisions.
contexts.original_text: In his seminal work [17], Kruchten introduced an ontology of ADDs in software-intensive systems. He classified ADDs into three main categories – existence decisions, property decisions, and executive decisions. Figure 2 shows the taxonomy of the ADD categories with the emphasis on existence decisions, which is the focus of our proposed approach.

contexts.name: Two-phase machine learning approach for design decision extraction and classification
contexts.description: A novel approach that automatically detects design decisions from issues in issue management systems and classifies them into decision categories such as structural, behavioral, and ban decisions.
contexts.original_text: First, we propose a two-phase machine learning (ML) based approach (cf. Fig. 1). In the first phase, design decisions are automatically detected from issues that are extracted from an issue management system. In the second phase, the identified design decisions are further classified into different decision categories.

contexts.text: Decision making for smart cities through KPIs assessment is challenging due to the complexity of smart cities as systems of systems with different dimensions managed by diverse stakeholders who do not always communicate, and the rigidity and lack of openness of current KPIs assessment frameworks.
contexts.original_text: However, decision making for smart cities through KPIs assessment is a quite challenging task. This is also due to the complexity of smart cities that are, de facto, systems of systems involving different dimensions (e.g., mobility, environment, education), each managed by different stakeholders, from public administrations to private institutions, that not always communicate with each other. Moreover, despite the support provided by Information and Communications Technologies (ICT) in managing different aspects of complex systems, such as smart cities (e.g., [5]), the currently available frameworks for the KPIs assessment are too rigid, not easy to suit each specific smart city’s peculiarity, and often not released as open frameworks.

contexts.name: Model-based approach for automatic KPIs assessment in smart cities
contexts.description: A methodology allowing stakeholders to define, model, and measure KPIs of interest for their cities, supporting decision making, customization, and evolution of KPIs to suit heterogeneous smart cities.
contexts.original_text: In this context, we argue that a systematic methodology allowing smart cities stakeholders to easily define, model and measure the KPIs of interest for their cities, efficiently supporting the decision making process, is necessary. The methodology should further support the KPIs customization and evolution to suit the unique features of different and heterogeneous smart cities. In this direction, we defined a model-based approach for the automatic KPIs assessment in smart cities as an effective instrument for smart governance enabling the stakeholders knowledge sharing, data interpretation and smart cities evaluation and comparison.

contexts.name: Flexible software architecture for KPIs assessment
contexts.description: An architecture supporting the model-based approach that identifies required and optional components and functionalities, allowing different deployment patterns and technology-independent components to suit various implementation needs.
contexts.original_text: In this paper, we present a flexible architecture supporting the model-based approach for KPIs assessment in smart cities that identifies both required and optional components and corresponding functionalities needed for realizing the automatic KPIs assessment approach, while showing two main flexibility points allowing for different specification of the architecture, thus of the overall methodology implementation. The flexibility is given by (i) different deployment patterns that can be followed for specifying the architecture (e.g., standalone, hybrid, online); (ii) the technology-independent nature of the shaped components, which enables the use of diverse technologies for implementing the designed architectural components, to also better suit the chosen deployment style (i.e., online modeling editors better suit in online deployment of the system).

contexts.name: Standalone specification of the architecture
contexts.description: A prototype implementation of the architecture as a standalone platform using Eclipse Modeling Framework (EMF), with graphical and textual editors for smart city and KPIs modeling, an evaluation engine implemented in Epsilon Object Language (EOL), and results export via Acceleo.
contexts.original_text: In this section, we present implementation details about the prototype we developed, corresponding to a standalone specification, being the architecture entirely implemented as a standalone platform. Eclipse is the release platform we have chosen, which also provides pre-packaged bundles for specific development paradigms. Specifically, the target platform is represented by the Eclipse Modeling Framework (EMF) that provides the modeling language to engineer DSLs. The EMF core includes a metamodeling language, called Ecore, used for describing domain models, and runtime support for the models including change notification, persistence support with default serialization, and reflective APIs for manipulating objects in the models. On top of the EMF bundle, the Metamodeling component (2) has been defined and it hosts the two main domain models ((2.a) and (2.b)) from which the Java code, supporting model manipulation and editors composition, is generated. On top of this layer, two editors are implemented ((3.a) and (3.b)) to better cope with the composition of the involved models, such as the editing of models with the possibility of filling them with model elements that can be composed. The editors implementation is supported by DSLs that, in general, can be graphical or textual. From one side, graphical editors provide an intuitive GUI for modelers. On the other side, textual editors provide a support tool to define models as textual specification, which is better transposed by developers. In order to enable the usage of the editors by both experienced and non-expert users (e.g., smart cities stakeholders), the component (3) is implemented with two different technologies. The Smart City Modeling Editor (3.a) is built on top of Sirius, a graphical concrete syntax generator creating the graphical modeling workbench for modeling smart cities. Smart city projects are quite large and involve different aspects and view points; since Sirius is based on a view points approach, it suits perfectly in this case. The KPI Modeling Editor (3.b), instead, is devised for modelers supporting KPIs experts to specify KPIs and relative calculation formulas. For this reason it has been implemented with a textual concrete syntax by means of Xtext. Xtext was chosen because it provides much more “expressiveness” and “agility” to the users, which can edit raw data in a very feasible way. The KPI Modeling Editor offers a way to declare how KPIs are calculated in detail, in the perspective of reuse, where the modelers can share their definitions. Lastly, the KPIs Fragment Selection/Customization Editor (3.c) is implemented by means of a custom reusable mechanism offered by Xtext. In particular, if the KPIs are declared as “reusable operations” in a library, the users can invoke the KPIs needed through this library. When the SC model and KPIs model have been defined, then the Analysis component (4) can be invoked, thus triggering the KPIs evaluation phase. This process is managed by the Requests Manager (1.a) that is implemented as an Eclipse plugin organized with the extension point mechanism. It can be activated by file saving operations or even directly by menu entries in the editors. By selecting a SC model and a KPIs model (with specific extensions), a menu entry is enabled and the EOL script implementing the Evaluation Engine (4.a) is triggered. The Epsilon Object Language (EOL) is an imperative programming language part of the Epsilon framework for creating, querying and modifying models built on top of EMF. Basically, the EOL script is a file in the workspace of the project that will be invoked by the plugin. The Evaluation Engine generates the evaluated KPIs model and the result will be also printed in the output console of Eclipse. The stakeholders can then request the visualization of the results in two different ways: by inspecting the textual result in the console or by asking to the Results Exporter (4.b) to generate an .xls file from the evaluated KPIs model. The excel file will be produced by a model-to-text transformation, from the Results Exporter implemented in Acceleo, i.e., one of the most used tools for code generation in MDE.

contexts.text: Practitioners struggle with creating and evolving an architecture when developing complex and safety-critical systems in large-scale agile contexts, particularly balancing upfront planning and flexibility to embrace change, and coordinating interfaces between components developed by multiple teams.
contexts.original_text: Practitioners struggle with creating and evolving an architecture when developing complex and safety-critical systems in large-scale agile contexts. A key issue is the trade-off between upfront planning and flexibility to embrace change. In particular, the coordination of interfaces is an important challenge, as interfaces determine and regulate the exchange of information between components, subsystems, and systems, which are often developed by multiple teams.

contexts.text: Coordination of interfaces is a significant challenge as they regulate information exchange between components developed by multiple teams, requiring better understanding and practical guidance.
contexts.original_text: In particular, the coordination of interfaces is an important challenge, as interfaces determine and regulate the exchange of information between components, subsystems, and systems, which are often developed by multiple teams. In a fast-changing environment, boundary objects between teams can provide the sufficient stability to align software or systems, while maintaining a sufficient degree of autonomy. However, a better understanding of interfaces as boundary objects is needed to give practical guidance.

contexts.name: Agile Architecture
contexts.description: The practice of developing software and systems architecture in a flexible, iterative manner that embraces change, especially in large-scale agile development contexts.
contexts.original_text: The interaction of software and systems architecture with agile development has received increased attention in the last decades. A core challenge with architecture in agile development is to deal with the tension between upfront architectural planning and agile development embracing change.

contexts.name: Interfaces
contexts.description: Boundaries that determine and regulate the exchange of information between components, subsystems, or systems, often developed by different teams, acting as boundary objects to provide stability and coordination.
contexts.original_text: Interfaces determine and regulate how two or more entities exchange information. Oftentimes, the entities connected by an interface are developed by different teams. To enable teams to work in an agile way, islands of stability are needed, which can be facilitated by the creation of boundary objects that maintain a common identity.

contexts.name: Identification of Dimensions Impacting Interface Change
contexts.description: The study identifies multiple measurable dimensions that impact how interfaces are changed in agile automotive contexts, such as criticality, number of affected components, time to perform a change, and level of abstraction, and explains their interrelations.
contexts.original_text: We identified several dimensions of interfaces and relationships between them. We consider dimensions as measurable characteristics of interfaces and how they are changed. An overview of our findings is displayed in Figure 1. The arrows represent implications between dimensions and the dimensions are directly proportional to each other.

contexts.name: Categorization of Interfaces in Agile Automotive Contexts
contexts.description: The study categorizes interfaces into three relevant categories: commodity interfaces, early stage interfaces, and central vehicle interfaces, based on identified dimensions and their characteristics.
contexts.original_text: We found three relevant categories along the identified dimensions: (i) commodity interfaces, (ii) early stage interfaces, and (iii) central vehicle interfaces.

contexts.name: Suggestions for Managing Interfaces in Large-Scale Agile Development
contexts.description: The paper proposes practices to manage different categories of interfaces, such as leaving stable and flexibly changeable interfaces to teams, controlling change for central vehicle interfaces, establishing interfaces to create boundaries, setting high abstraction levels, and assessing interfaces early on.
contexts.original_text: We propose to leave stable and flexibly changeable interfaces up to the teams, but to control change for central vehicle interfaces. For all categories, we advise to establish interfaces to create boundaries that enable independent development, set an interfaces abstraction level as high as possible, and to assess interfaces early on.

contexts.text: The paper addresses the problem of how proprietary Embedded Software Development Environments and Toolsets (ESDTs) provided by MCU manufacturers impose architecturally significant constraints on embedded software architecture, which are often communicated inappropriately to engineering teams, leading to difficulties in software reuse and migration to new hardware platforms.
contexts.original_text: This selection is driven by business, technical, organizational, and legal constraints. Often, the hardware is delivered together with proprietary environments in which the software to be deployed has to be developed. This imposes architecturally significant constraints that are usually communicated inappropriately (in terms of time and format) to the engineering team. Examples are the usage of proprietary data types and programming language constructs (e.g., macros in C) and limitations to the reuse of existing software assets.

contexts.text: There is a challenge in managing the influence of proprietary ESDTs on embedded systems software architecture, especially since generic ESDTs are not yet feasible due to strong hardware-software coupling.
contexts.original_text: Although ESDTs influence the software architecture, they are hardware-specific, and their influence is commonly neglected by existing approaches. Ideally, hardware-independent and generic ESDTs would resolve this issue. However, previous research (e.g., Bulajic et al. 3 , Yagi et al. 4 , Hussein et al. 5 ) has identified several major challenges for the development of generic ESDTs. The origin of these challenges is the strong coupling between embedded software and specific hardware.

contexts.text: There is a lack of formal methods to manage hardware and ESDT dependencies of software and to guide the MCU selection process considering software architecture constraints.
contexts.original_text: Since it is clear that in most cases engineers need to use either limited in-house or provided manufacturer-specific ESDTs, there is a great need for solutions to manage hardware and ESDT dependencies of software. There is also a need to formally manage the hardware selection process (specifically the selection of the MCU) while taking into account its ramifications regarding ESDTs, embedded system architecture parts influenced by ESDTs, and hence the complete software engineering process influenced by these factors.

contexts.text: There is a lack of explicit expression and management of software architecture dependencies on manufacturer-specific ESDTs, which complicates future migrations and software reuse.
contexts.original_text: Besides this initial guidance, there is a strong need to explicitly express the dependencies of the software architecture on manufacturer-specific ESDTs in order to ease future migrations. Therefore, we suggest an extension view to the SPES-1-based Embedded Modeling Profile: an embedded system ESDT dependency (SED) architecture view.

contexts.name: Embedded Software Development Environments and Toolsets (ESDT)
contexts.description: Integrated development systems provided by MCU manufacturers including IDE, proprietary compilers, build systems, data types, programming constraints, and libraries that influence embedded software architecture.
contexts.original_text: Hardware manufacturers, especially manufacturers of MicroController Units (MCU), tend to provide Embedded Software Development environments and Toolsets (ESDT). An ESDT comprises an integrated development system (i.e., IDE), a proprietary compiler, build systems, proprietary data types and programming constraints, and libraries, among others.

contexts.name: Bare-metal systems
contexts.description: Embedded systems without an operating system abstraction layer, characterized by direct hardware access and resource scarcity, which affect software engineering.
contexts.original_text: An additional challenge in embedded systems is the tight coupling of hardware and software, which occurs predominantly in bare-metal systems (i.e., with no abstraction layer introduced by the operating system). The lack of the insulating layer provided by the operating system (i) changes the hardware abstraction view and (ii) allows direct hardware access to peripheral devices. Bare-metal systems are often characterized by (iii) considerable resource scarcity.

contexts.name: SPES modeling framework
contexts.description: A widely accepted architecture-centric engineering framework for embedded systems, on top of which customized frameworks like Fraunhofer Embedded Modeling Profile (EMP) are designed.
contexts.original_text: Architecture-centric techniques have played a key role in managing the inherent complexity of Embedded Systems Engineering. For example, the SPES 1 modeling framework is a widely accepted approach for architecture-centric engineering of embedded systems on top of which more customized frameworks, like the Fraunhofer Embedded Modeling Profile (EMP) 2 have been designed.
