contexts.text: Challenges in large data computation for plant genotyping and phenotyping, including reproducibility, high throughput processing of heterogeneous data, metadata identification, and data management.
contexts.original_text: There are a number of challenges involved in automating the process of plant genotyping and phenotyping, e.g. reproducibility of experiments, high throughput processing of large amounts of data in various formats (e.g. structured, semi-structured and unstructured), identification of appropriate meta-data for the diverse uses of the data, collecting, abstracting, and loading data into easily accessible structures.

contexts.text: Existing plant genotyping and phenotyping systems have shortcomings such as limited support for high throughput processing of large heterogeneous data and lack of flexibility for advanced features.
contexts.original_text: Our SAAM analysis shows that the existing systems have shortcomings. For example, they are limited in their support for high throughput processing of large amounts of heterogeneous types of data.

contexts.text: No existing cloud-based reference architecture for plant genotyping and phenotyping that supports data-centric, software component, and infrastructure models.
contexts.original_text: To the best of our knowledge no cloud-based reference architecture exists in the subject domain that can handle the data centric, software component and infrastructure models.

contexts.text: Need for a reference architecture to guide developers and architects in designing plant genotyping and phenotyping systems that meet scalability, reusability, and composability requirements.
contexts.original_text: Based on our findings we propose a reference architecture along with a preliminary evaluation in the subject domain. The reference architecture and its evaluation is aimed at helping developers architects create suitable architectural designs and select appropriate technologies when developing plant phenotyping and genotyping systems.

contexts.name: Technical Debt (TD)
contexts.description: Design or implementation constructs that are expedient in the short term but can make future changes more costly or impossible, impacting internal system qualities like maintainability and evolvability.
contexts.original_text: In software-intensive systems, technical debt consists of design or implementation constructs that are expedient in the short term, but set up a technical context that can make a future change more costly or impossible. Technical debt is a contingent liability whose impact is limited to internal system qualities, primarily maintainability and evolvability.

contexts.name: Architectural Technical Debt (ATD)
contexts.description: Technical debt incurred at the architectural level of software design, including decisions related to structure, technologies, development process, and platform, which can limit future evolution or cause quality issues and delays.
contexts.original_text: Our focus is on Architectural Technical Debt (ATD). This is the technical debt incurred at the architectural level of software design, i.e., in the decisions related to structure (layering, decomposition in subsystems, interfaces), technologies (frameworks, packages, libraries, deployment approach), or even languages, development process, and platform. As software systems grow in size and their lifespan extends, many of these original design choices become constraints, limiting future evolution or even preventing it. To evolve the system, developers find workarounds, introducing quality issues and delays.

contexts.name: Grounded Theory (GT)
contexts.description: A research method that lets concepts emerge from data collected from participants' experiences, avoiding preconceived views and prior knowledge influence.
contexts.original_text: We used a grounded theory approach [12] with experienced industry practitioners as subjects. ... We adopted the classic “Glaserian” Grounded Theory (GT) method [12], and we stayed with it throughout the whole study, from data collection, to data analysis and synthesis, with the exception of our adoption of a different “coding family” w.r.t. the ones suggested by Glaser [11]. This GT approach has given us a fresh and independent viewpoint on ATD, by letting concepts emerge from the personal experience of our participants, rather than the preconceived views of the researchers. In line with GT principles, we delayed the review of the literature until after our theory emerged, in order to avoid the influence of existing concepts on our theory [10].

contexts.text: The complexity and error-proneness of functional interconnection and data routing in today's automotive electronic architectures hinder short development-to-operation times.
contexts.original_text: The functional interconnection and data routing in todays automotive electric electronic architectures has reached a level of complexity which is hardly manageable and error-prone. This circumstance severely hinders short times from development to operation.

contexts.text: Current ECU- or signal-based development approaches have reached their limits in managing complexity and ensuring data consistency and completeness.
contexts.original_text: ECU- or signal-based development approaches are the predominant ones today and have reached their limits of mastering complexity. Data maintenance of signal and bus message databases requires a lot of time and money. Nonetheless, data consistency and completeness cannot be guaranteed.

contexts.original_text: The purpose of the study is to evaluate the feasibility of Data Distribution Services in accord with containerization technologies in an agile development process for automotive software.

contexts.name: Data Distribution Service (DDS)
contexts.description: A data-centric publish-subscribe middleware standard designed for real-time and data-critical communication, supporting Quality of Service (QoS) policies, high reliability, availability, automatic failover, and redundancy.
contexts.original_text: DDS 9 is a data-centric publish-subscribe (DCPS) middleware standard. DCPS describes communication between two parties as the exchange of data via services: An information holder, the publisher publishes the data via a single or multiple topics. A data requesting participant, the subscriber, subscribes to one of these topics to receive the data. ... DDS has been developed with the following design goals in mind: (i) high reliability and availability, (ii) automatic failover, and (iii) redundancy.

contexts.name: Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA)
contexts.description: An architectural style where software functions are provided as reusable services with clear interfaces, facilitating reuse, clear documentation, and encapsulation of independent behavior.
contexts.original_text: In a service-oriented architecture (SOA), such communal infrastructure functions can be provided as a service and be reused. ... With the introduction of a service-oriented architecture in automotive E E systems, considerable benefits are brought: (i) a hierarchical in-vehicle function- software architecture is realized; (ii) a clear and explicit documentation of service and thus functional interdependencies is given; (iii) SOA facilitates reuse of functionality; (iv) a data-centric publish- subscribe mechanism pushes the practitioners focus on data rather than actions; (v) a clear encapsulation of independent behavior is given (high cohesion and low coupling).

contexts.description: A technology that packages applications and their dependencies into isolated, lightweight containers sharing the host OS kernel, enabling fast deployment, continuous integration, and flexible service repartitioning.
contexts.original_text: Containers are independent units of deployment containing everything a particular application needs to run from system libraries, tools, and runtimes to application spe- cific settings. ... contexts.name: Safety analysis of cooperative adaptive cruise control system using fault tree analysis and fault classification methods
contexts.description: Developed an architectural model of a cooperative adaptive cruise control system and analyzed its functional safety, showing that cooperative architecture affects safety goals due to vehicle-to-vehicle communication faults.
contexts.original_text: The architectural model of a cooperative adaptive cruise control system is developed and its functional safety is analyzed using a combination of fault tree analysis and fault classification methods. The results show that inclusion of cooperative architecture perspective affects the safety goals of cooperative adaptive cruise control because ASIL determination is influenced by vehicle-to-vehicle communication faults.

contexts.text: Architectural decay causes increased developer effort, system correctness issues, and performance degradation, which manifest as implementation issues over time.
contexts.original_text: Architectural decay imposes real costs in terms of developer effort, system correctness, and performance. Over time, those problems are likely to be revealed as explicit implementation issues (defects, feature changes, etc.).

contexts.text: Existing code-level prediction techniques do not adequately address architectural-level issues, despite architectural decay being a significant source of technical debt and implementation problems.
contexts.original_text: In contrast to code-level techniques, analogous techniques at the architecture level have not received nearly as much attention, even though recent work has demonstrated that even simple code updates can cause system-wide architectural changes. Frequently, such updates introduce architectural smells in a system (e.g., dependency cycle, ambiguous interface). These smells may have no immediately visible effect, but they are symptoms of architectural decay and accumulated technical debt.

contexts.text: The distribution of issues and changes per file in software systems follows a heavy-tailed pattern, necessitating segmentation into low, medium, and high proneness levels for better estimation of architectural decay impact.
contexts.original_text: where many files are associated with small numbers of issues and code changes, while comparatively fewer files are associ- ated with large numbers of issues and changes. This is not an uncommon type of distribution 72 , 8 . As an illustration, the Pareto chart 68 in Figure 3 depicts the distribution of issues per file in Hadoop: while few files are associated with a large number of issues, the arc, which represents the cumulative per- centage of file-groups sizes, shows a clear heavy-tailed pattern. One common labeling approach is to segment a heavy-tailed distribution into head and tail segments. A more sophisticated approach is to divide the distribution into three partshead, body, and tailwhich in our case represent the three levels of proneness: low, medium, and high. We choose the latter approach because the numerical values in our study span a wide range. Having these three levels gives developers a better estimation of architectural decays impact.

contexts.text: Balancing datasets with imbalanced class distributions is necessary to avoid biased prediction models, achieved here using SMOTE to oversample medium and high proneness labels to equalize class ratios.
contexts.original_text: Due to the distribution of data and the labeling approach, we need to balance our datasets 55 . Recall from Section III-B2 that the low : med : high ratio of our datasets is 80:16:4 (i.e., 20:4:1). If such a dataset were used to train a prediction model, the most likely outcome would be a model that predicts low for every data point. As we are more interested in high and med labels, such a model would be useless. It is thus important to ensure that weighted metrics are not biased by less (or more) frequent labels. We use SMOTE 11 to balance our dataset, oversampling med by a factor of 5 and high by a factor of 20. SMOTE is a technique that synthesizes new minority samples based on nearest neighbors between sample data points. Adding new minority samples guarantees that the dataset will be balanced, i.e., that the low : med : high ratio will be 1:1:1.

contexts.text: Prediction models using architectural smells as features can accurately predict issue-proneness and change-proneness of software system files, outperforming baseline random models significantly.
contexts.original_text: Our results confirm that architectural smell-based models can accurately predict the issue-proneness of a system. In other words, architectural smells have a consistent impact on a systems implementation with respect to issue-proneness over the systems lifetime. This finding means that architectural decay can be a powerful indicator of the health of a systems implementation. It serves as a direct motivator for software engineers to pay more attention to the architecture, and architectural smells, in their systems. For example, system maintainers can use our models to foresee future problems, to devise refactoring plans, to prioritize their activities, etc.

contexts.text: Historical data of architectural smells, issues, and changes can be used to develop models that accurately predict issue- and change-proneness of software systems throughout their lifetimes.
contexts.original_text: In summary, our results confirm that the historical data of a software system regarding its architectural smells, issues, and changes can be used to develop models to accurately predict the issue- and change-proneness of that system. The results also indicate that architectural smells have a consistent impact on software system implementations throughout the systems lifetimes.

contexts.text: Selecting appropriate architecture recovery techniques (ACDC and ARC) improves prediction model performance compared to PKG.
contexts.original_text: Lastly, ACDC and ARC outperform PKG, emphasizing the importance of selecting the appropriate architecture recovery techniques and targeting them to the task at hand.

contexts.text: Unrelated software systems tend to share properties regarding issue- and change-proneness, allowing models trained on multiple systems to predict properties of systems lacking historical data, though with some accuracy loss.
contexts.original_text: The results of the experiments conducted in the context of RQ2 confirm that software systems tend to share properties with respect to issue- and change-proneness. The accuracy of general-purpose models is lower than that of specific models, but the gap is not prohibitive. Our results suggest that developers can use general-purpose models to get an overall sense of the likely issue- and change-proneness of a new software system in the early stages of its development, before sufficiently large numbers of system versions become available. Similarly, developers can use such models to predict important properties of any existing systems for which historical data is missing, spotty, or unreliable.

contexts.text: Collaborative design by multiple architects often leads to design conflicts that hinder collaboration and cause wasted effort.
contexts.original_text: In collaborative design, architects individual design decisions may conflict and, when joined, may violate system con- sistency rules or non-functional requirements. These design con- flicts can hinder collaboration and result in wasted effort.

contexts.text: Proactive detection of design conflicts is computationally expensive, limiting its practical applicability.
contexts.original_text: Proac- tive detection of code-level conflicts has been shown to improve collaborative productivity; however, the computational resource requirements for proactively computing design conflicts have hin- dered its applicability in practice.

contexts.text: Version control systems detect synchronization conflicts only at synchronization time and miss high-order conflicts until after merging, causing rework and lost context.
contexts.original_text: Unfortunately, VCSs help to discover synchronization design conflicts only when the architects synchronize, and high-order design conflicts after synchronization and after the architects elect to run their analyses. This can lead to design and im- plementation work that repeatedly needs to be corrected, even abandoned, which becomes more difficult when engineers for- get the context of their initial decisions because of the time lag.

contexts.text: Continuous proactive conflict detection at the design level is expensive and can slow architects' tools, requiring prioritization and distribution of computational load.
contexts.original_text: Unfortunately, unlike code-level conflict detection, continuous proactive con- flict detection (PCD) at the design-level may be prohibitively expensive. Many design analyses are highly computation in- tensive, including, e.g., discrete-event simulation 52 , Markov- chain-based reliability analysis 59 , queueing-network-based performance analysis 4 , and symbolic model checking 15 . Running such analyses locally on an architects machine may slow the architects tools, and delayed conflict discovery may lead to decisions that must be reversed later. Slow analyses further exacerbate the problem by allowing more pending anal- ysis instances to queue up. Thus, for PCD to be useful, it must prioritize and distribute the computational load (1) to deliver analysis results quickly and (2) to avoid detrimentally impacting the architects use of her tools.

contexts.name: Queue prioritization algorithm
contexts.description: A novel prioritization algorithm that bounds the time required to detect high-order design conflicts to twice the running time of the analysis, by processing the newest model representations first.
contexts.original_text: FLAME implements a novel prioritization algorithm for selecting which representations to analyze first. This algorithm bounds the time required to detect the high-order design conflicts to twice the running time of the analysis that finds the conflict. The algorithm takes advantage of FLAMEs operation-based granularity and processes the chronologically newest conflict detection instances first, without any loss of the collaboratively generated design information.

contexts.text: The implementation of software systems often diverges from the intended architecture including its security measures, leading to severe vulnerabilities that are hard to fix.
contexts.original_text: However, the implementation often diverges from this intended architecture including its security measures. This may lead to severe vulnerabilities that have a wide impact on the system and are hard to fix afterwards.

contexts.text: Existing architectural conformance checking approaches have limitations: they mostly focus on structural rules and static analysis, neglecting behavioral rules, dynamic sources, and artifacts beyond source code, which are essential for security analysis.
contexts.original_text: We identified three issues when using these approaches for architectural security rules: Most approaches concentrate on structural rules but do not consider system behavior. As behavioral rules are essential for security this may cause undetected software vulnerabilities (Issue 1). Most conformance checking techniques base on static analysis of source code. They do not consider dynamically loaded sources and content which are important for a security analysis (Issue 2). Existing conformance checking approaches do rarely consider artifact beyond source code. However, considering additional source artifact such as configuration settings and their impact on the system behavior is essential when conducting a security analysis (Issue 3).

contexts.text: There is a major security knowledge gap among software engineers, which challenges the development of secure software systems.
contexts.original_text: Knowledge There is a major security knowledge gap among software engineers 3 . To meet this challenge in developing secure software systems, we build on an existing controlled natural language approach: As the ArchCNL support is based on Xtext, we could extend it to support the TArchCNLs temporal operators and improved variable handling.

contexts.text: Continuous conformance checks are necessary to monitor adherence to architectural security rules, requiring integration into processes and regular review activities.
contexts.original_text: To monitor the adherence to architectural security rules, continuous conformance checks are necessary: The architect needs to integrate the security conformance checks into processes and regular review activities.

contexts.text: Existing architectural security rules are mostly derived from well-established security patterns and principles and are applicable across many projects, with behavioral rules being particularly important for security.
contexts.original_text: The architectural security rules presented by Jasser 3 have been derived from well-established architectural security measures and knowledge such as pattern, tactics and practices. Most of the rules based on security principles or common flaws, respectively, could be applied to our case study along with rules derived from patterns that were used. We did not find any project-specific rules. It is most likely, that the common architectural security rules may be used in many projects. However, we assess rules derived from design flaws most important as they indicate violations of security principles that affect almost all software systems. Further, our case study verified that behavioral rules are of particular importance for security and should therefore be promoted.

contexts.text: Architectural security rules increase awareness among software engineers and architects and help reduce the abstraction gap between high-level security measures and code-level implementation, but their benefit is limited without appropriate enforcement approaches.
contexts.original_text: The high number of architectural security rule violations we found in our case study illustrate the importance of architectural security rules. The rules increase the awareness of software engineers and architects. They also may help reducing the abstraction gap between high level security measures and their code-level implementation. However, as the rules are not specified explicitly in most cases, their benefit is limited without appropriate enforcement approaches. Hence, we consider it necessary to complement architectural security rules with tool-supported conformance checking approaches.

contexts.name: Linear Time Logic (LTL)
contexts.description: A formalism used to express temporal properties referring to future states, enabling the modeling of temporal aspects in security architectural rules.
contexts.original_text: The formalization of security architectural rules requires to consider temporal aspects. contexts.name: Architecture Concept Language Flexibility
contexts.description: The ability of TArchCNL to allow architects to flexibly specify architectural security concepts and roles using project-specific terminology, supporting structural, behavioral, and data flow related rules.
contexts.original_text: Architects can flexibly specify architectural security concepts such as AuthorizationMechanism, User or SensitiveData and roles like log or encrypt. They are free to choose terms for the architectural security concepts and roles based on the language that is used within the project and, hence, well understood by the project developers. TArchCNL allows to define structural, behavioral and data flow related rules that constrain these concepts.

contexts.text: Writing Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) is challenging due to the need to blend different specialized infrastructure programming languages and abstractions, especially for complex Data-Intensive Architectures (DIAs).
contexts.original_text: Writing IaC, however, is not an easy task, since it requires blending different infrastructure programming languages and abstrac- tions, each specialized on a particular aspect of infrastructure creation, configuration, and management.

contexts.text: The complexity and size of architectures like DIAs increase the need for IaC, but the diversity of languages and tools required makes IaC development difficult and under-utilized in many companies.
contexts.original_text: Moreover, the more the architectures become large and complex (e.g. Data-Intensive or Microservice-based architectures), the more dire the need of IaC becomes.

contexts.text: IaC development requires specialized skills across various domains and tools, which many companies lack, limiting the automation potential of IaC.
contexts.original_text: Such diversity implies that adopting the IaC approach today requires a variety of specialised skills that, in many cases, average companies do not have and struggle to find. For this reason, the huge automation potential offered by IaC remains under-utilised.

contexts.text: Manual deployment and configuration of DIAs is time-consuming and error-prone, requiring highly skilled engineers and involving manual interventions that increase the risk of errors.
contexts.original_text: NETF measured the time needed for a complete manual deployment and configuration of their DIA. Such process was conducted by a software engineer highly skilled in Linux and in Java and took exactly 63 working hours... some of the deployment steps currently require human manual intervention on the nodes (VMs) which is usually an error prone process.

contexts.text: Current deployment processes for Big Data applications lack automation tools, making deployment slow and complex compared to other application domains like mobile or web applications.
contexts.original_text: According to NETF, this time was mainly due to the lack of tools for tasks automation. NETF highlighted that, a mobile application developer can write the code, compile, deploy and simulate his her application by simply pushing the Run button. A similar situation occurs in the case of web applications, while this is currently not possible for Big Data application developers.

contexts.text: Complex Big Data applications require developers to manually manage the entire development cycle, including fine tuning and controlling multiple aspects to meet critical Quality of Service (QoS) requirements.
contexts.original_text: NETF also argued that for complex applications like Big Data ones, developers have to manually deal with the whole development cycle, as there are several aspects to fine tune and keep under control to ensure the fulfillment of the critical QoS requirements.

contexts.text: Re-deployment of DIAs is time-consuming, with expert engineers requiring several hours to complete the process manually.
contexts.original_text: ATC declared previous experience in deployment of DIA frameworks and declared that a complete re-deployment of their DIA currently takes around 4 hours of work of an expert engineer.

contexts.name: Cloud Orchestrators and TOSCA
contexts.description: Tools and standards for service provisioning and application deployment in cloud environments, with TOSCA being an OASIS standard for orchestration languages.
contexts.original_text: Server provisioning entails acquiring (e.g. from a public provider of Infrastructure-as-a-Service), configuring and running the required VMs or containers upon which services can run. Application deployment is the phase in which users applications are executed on the resulting infrastructure. Configuration management is typically handled by well-known tools like Chef, Puppet, Ansible, while service provisioning and application deployment are responsibilities of so called Cloud orchestrators. In this area, TOSCA is the Topology and Orchestration Specification for Cloud Applications and is the reference OASIS standard for orchestration languages.

contexts.name: DICER Approach
contexts.description: A model-driven engineering approach that creates language-agnostic models for Data-Intensive Architectures and automatically transforms them into Infrastructure-as-Code, simplifying IaC design and reducing deployment times.
contexts.original_text: The goal of this paper is to exploit Model- Driven Engineering (MDE) to create language-agnostic models that are then automatically transformed into IaC. ... we show that, through our approach, called DICER, it is possible to create complex IaC with significant amounts of time savings, both in IaC design as well as deployment and re-deployment times.

contexts.text: There is considerable uncertainty and risk in architecting microservice data management due to inconsistent, incomplete, and experience-based practices reported mainly in grey literature.
contexts.original_text: Most of the established practices in industry are only reported in the so-called 7rey literature8, consisting of practitioner blogs, experience reports, system documentations, etc. In most cases, each of these sources documents a few existing practices well, but usually they do not provide systematic architectural guidance. Instead the reported practices are largely based on personal experience, often inconsistent, and, when studied on their own, incomplete. This creates considerable uncertainty and risk in architecting microservice data management, which can be reduced either through substantial personal experience or by a careful study of a large set of knowledge sources.

contexts.text: The paper addresses the challenge of architecting data management in microservice architectures, which involves complex issues such as data integrity, querying, transaction management, and consistency due to decentralized data management.
contexts.original_text: Some of these tenets introduce substantial challenges for the data management architecture. Notably, it is usually advised to decentralize all data management concerns. Such an architecture requires, in addition to the already existing non-trivial design challenges intrinsic in distributed systems, sophisticated solutions for data integrity, data querying, transaction management, and consistency management [14, 15, 18, 20].

contexts.text: There is a lack of systematic architectural guidance for microservice data management practices, as most existing knowledge is scattered in grey literature and based on personal experience, leading to uncertainty and risk in architecture design.
contexts.original_text: Many authors have written about microservice data management and various attempts to document microservice patterns and best practices exist [8, 12, 15, 18]. Nevertheless, most of the established practices in industry are only reported in the so-called 7rey literature8, consisting of practitioner blogs, experience reports, system documentations, etc. In most cases, each of these sources documents a few existing practices well, but usually they do not provide systematic architectural guidance. Instead the reported practices are largely based on personal experience, often inconsistent, and, when studied on their own, incomplete. This creates considerable uncertainty and risk in architecting microservice data management, which can be reduced either through substantial personal experience or by a careful study of a large set of knowledge sources.

contexts.name: Database per Service pattern
contexts.description: A microservice data management pattern where each microservice manages its own data and communicates with others only through well-defined APIs, promoting loose coupling and independent scalability.
contexts.original_text: By definition, a microservice should be autonomous, loosely coupled and able to be developed, deployed, and scaled independently. This is ensured by the Database per Service pattern, which we encountered, either directly or implicitly, in 33 out of 35 sources: each microservice manages its own data, and data exchange and communications with other services are realized only through a set of well-defined APIs.

contexts.text: The automotive industry is investing in autonomous vehicles at SAE level 3, which requires the vehicle to manage dynamic driving tasks independently, posing challenges in software complexity and computational demands.
contexts.original_text: The automotive industry is currently investing considerable efforts and resources towards the achievement of an autonomous vehicle that would meet the specification of SAE level 3�[18]. Several companies have in fact already marketed vehicles exhibiting different semi-autonomous capabilities belonging to SAE level 2, ranging from adaptive lane keeping to self-parking features. The most relevant difference between level 2 and 3 in the SAE hierarchy is on who takes the responsibility of monitoring the driving environment: while in SAE level 2 the system assists the human driver in latitudinal and longitudinal adjustments, it is the driver who is expected to perform all the remaining tasks; instead, in SAE level 3 this is not required, meaning that the vehicle itself should be able to manage the dynamic driving tasks while the human driver is only expected to intervene upon request�[17].The software necessary to manage the diversity of situations that a vehicle can face is bound to be complex and computationally intensive, especially considering that the software present in modern vehicles already exceeds the Gigabyte in size�[11]. Moreover, as all vehicles share the same basic capabilities but differ in the provided software functionality, it can be expected that the latter will constitute for the customers a relevant practical difference between automakers, thus fuelling a functionality race that will move the value concentration from the hardware, i.e.,�the vehicle itself, to its software capabilities.

contexts.text: The automotive industry faces challenges in implementing Continuous Experimentation in vehicles due to limited computational resources, the complexity of cyber-physical systems, and the need for remote software deployment and data collection.
contexts.original_text: Continuous Experimentation has proven to be very effective on web-based software systems [10]. However, applying verbatim this way of working onto safety-critical cyber-physical systems such as vehicles would be an endeavour destined to face the specific challenges of the automotive context. One challenge is the added complexity given by the fact that the target systems in the case of vehicles are not virtual machines in server farms but highly mobile physical objects with limited computational performance. Moreover, there is a resource availability problem given by the Continuous Experimentation practice itself, which introduces a non-traditional approach when it comes to testing new functionality and needs additional computational power in order to manage the additional experiments and the data collection [9] on top of the system9s nominal functions. This can pose issues to the automotive industry, which, being based on an economy of scale, has always built vehicles with hardware that is just enough powerful to fulfill its tasks in order to lower production costs. It also requires a rethinking of the classic system and software9s architectures due to the new practice in which extra software is downloaded and run while its results are collected and uploaded back to the manufacturer.

contexts.name: Continuous Experimentation (CE)
contexts.description: A practice building upon CI/CD that enables developers to deploy and run multiple software experiments alongside official software to test new functionalities in real-world scenarios, making software evolution data-driven.
contexts.original_text: Continuous Experimentation builds upon the CI/CD pipeline and aims at enabling the developers to test new software performances by providing the possibility of deploying and running alongside the official software a number of experiments. These experiments could be either different versions of the official software or new functionality to be field-tested. While it adds computational overhead to the systems, Continuous Experimentation allows to confirm or reject hypotheses about the software suitability for a given task based on real-world data as opposed to simulations or speculations, making the software evolution process data-driven.

contexts.text: Software architects face various architectural design decisions when designing systems that link runtime events to model elements for model-based analysis, but there is no exhaustive list of solution alternatives or explicit trade-offs available.
contexts.original_text: However, software architects are confronted with various design decisions when designing a system that yields the required runtime events and correlates them to the model elements they originate from.

contexts.text: There is a lack of architectural guidance to help software architects balance trade-offs between solution alternatives for systems supporting model-based analysis of runtime events.
contexts.original_text: As a consequence, architectural guidance is needed to help software architects to balance the trade-offs between the various solution alternatives for recurring design situations when implementing systems with model-based analysis support.

contexts.text: Relating models and runtime behaviour for analysis at runtime is often neglected despite its potential benefits.
contexts.original_text: However, while the majority of model-driven approaches close the gap between the problem space and the solution space at design time, relating models and runtime behaviour, e.g., to analyze the running system from a high-level perspective, is often neglected.

contexts.text: Aspect-oriented techniques are performance-friendly for extracting events without changing original code, but dynamic variants need further analysis for performance under high event loads.
contexts.original_text: Aspect-oriented techniques turned out to be a performance- friendly solution for extracting events without the need of changes to the original code, but further analyses are needed to test if dynamic aspect-oriented programming variants (i.e., changing pointcuts and advices at runtime to meet changing monitoring requirements) can cope with the amount of events in terms of performance because they usually rely on additional runtime checks.

contexts.text: Using SQL or existing event processing languages for runtime event analysis requires maintaining additional resources and integration efforts.
contexts.original_text: For the analysis of runtime events, using SQL or other existing event processing languages is usually accompanied by maintaining additional resources (e.g., a database server) and additional integration issues.

contexts.text: Creating a custom analysis language involves initial effort but may reduce overall effort across multiple projects.
contexts.original_text: Creating an own analysis language is concerned with an initial effort, but may lead to an overall effort reduction if applied in multiple projects.

contexts.name: Model-based analysis
contexts.description: An approach where runtime events relevant to model elements are monitored and analyzed to understand the behavior of a running system at a high level, linking runtime events to model elements to perform aggregation and analysis.
contexts.original_text: The goal of model-based analysis is to monitor such runtime events that are relevant for the model elements of interest (e.g., the start and end events of a UML behaviour) and to perform the desired analysis based on those events (e.g., calculating the average runtime of the modelled UML behaviour using the time stamps of the start and end events).

contexts.original_text: We then performed initial steps towards a architectural guidance model by applying the taxonomy to another realistic scenario, following the Design Science Research method, in order to analyze the properties and deepen our own technical understanding of the captured concepts in the taxonomy.

contexts.name: Taxonomy validation and refinement through practical application
contexts.description: The taxonomy of architectural design decisions was validated and refined by applying it to practical systems, including a LEGO robot system designed by novice architects and the Mars Simulation Project, to observe properties and deepen understanding of architectural concepts.
contexts.original_text: We applied the directed content analysis method to the documentation artefacts produced by the architects... The mapping of the design decisions onto the initial taxonomy... gives us confidence that the taxonomy poses a suitable starting point for creating an architectural guidance model... For further refinement... we iteratively applied the captured techniques to the Mars Simulation Project according to the Design Science Research method... The techniques were applied in various combinations over the course of 12 iterations and the insights mainly their pros and cons recorded.

contexts.text: Checking whether a new version of a software component refines the behavior of its predecessor in terms of observable input-output behavior is crucial for stepwise refinement in software architecture development.
contexts.original_text: This requires means to check whether a new version of a component with potentially different interface and behavior implementation refines the behavior of its predecessor.

contexts.text: Existing architecture description languages (ADLs) have complex semantic domains that require partially manual proving to establish refinement between component versions, impeding automated stepwise refinement.
contexts.original_text: Where architecture description languages (ADLs) support refinement checking, the complexity of their semantic domain requires (partially) manual proving to establish refinement between component versions.

contexts.text: There is a need for a semantics domain and refinement checking method that is powerful enough to model complex systems yet supports fully automated refinement checking.
contexts.original_text: We identified a subset of the FOCUS semantics for describing distributed systems as stream processing functions that is powerful enough to model complex and realistic systems, yet sufficiently powerful to support fully automated refinement checking.

contexts.name: FOCUS semantics
contexts.description: A formal framework for describing distributed interactive systems as stream processing functions, used as a semantic domain for components.
contexts.original_text: We identified a subset of the FOCUS semantics for time-synchronous, distributed, interactive systems that is powerful enough to model complex and realistic systems and yet enables fully automated refinement checking between components.

contexts.name: Time-Synchronous Stream Processing Functions (TSSPFs)
contexts.description: Functions modeling component behavior by mapping input communication histories to output histories in discrete time units, ensuring causality and realizability.
contexts.original_text: We model the semantics of distributed interactive systems as sets of time-synchronous stream processing functions (TSSPFs). The notion of TSSPFs is inspired by the notion of timed SPFs.

contexts.name: Time-Synchronous Port Automata (TSPAs)
contexts.description: Automata inspired by port automata and IO automata that consume and output at most one message per input channel per time slice, with finite states and transitions, used to model component behavior with reactive transitions and defined operational and denotational semantics.
contexts.original_text: TSPAs as introduced in this paper are strongly inspired by port automata as introduced in 12 , I Oautomata as introduced in 27 , 24 , and MAAts automata as defined in 22 . Port and I Oautomata consume and produce time slices of arbitrary but finitely many input messages in every transition step. In contrast, TSPAs and MAAts automata consume and output at most one message per input channel in each time slice. Given the set of states and the channel types of an automaton are finite, MAAts automata and the automata presented here are guaranteed to have finitely many transitions. This is not the case for I Oand port automata since both have to define a transition for each state and each possible input communication history. Even if the type of a channel is finite, the number of communication histories (streams) of the channels type is infinite. I O and MAAts automata enforce causality between input and output histories by requiring initial outputs on all channels. In contrast, TSPAs do not require initial outputs. While the syntax of MAAts automata treat variables explicitly, variables have to be represented implicitly in the state space of TSPAs. TSPAs can be treated as a special case of port automata as presented in 12 . Thereby the proofs of many theorems presented in the following are analog to proofs, which have already been carried out in 12 . A TSPA consists of a set of states, an interface given by input and output channels, and transitions defining the TSPAs behavior. The interface is encoded by a port signature.

contexts.name: Reactivity of TSPAs
contexts.description: TSPAs must be reactive, meaning they define a reaction to every possible well-typed input in every state and time unit, performing exactly one state change and outputting exactly one message per output channel per time unit.
contexts.original_text: TSPAs must not block their environments and must be able to react to any possible well-typed input in any time unit. Therefore, a TSPA must define a reaction to every possible input for each of its states. The reactions of a TSPA are defined by its transitions. In each time unit, a TSPA performs exactly one state change by executing one transition enabled by its input and outputs exactly one message on each output channel.

contexts.name: Buchi Automata (BAs)
contexts.description: Finite automata accepting infinite words, used in model checking, defined by finite alphabets, states, initial and accepting states, and transitions, with acceptance based on infinite visits to accepting states.
contexts.original_text: B uchi automata 2 are a variant of finite automata that are acceptors for infinite words and thus induce languages consisting of infinite words. They are well known and much used in the model checking domain. Infinite words over an alphabet are infinite sequences of symbols in . The set of all infinite words over an alphabet is denoted by . Definition 17 (B uchi Automaton). A BA is a tuple (, Q, I, F, ) where is a finite alphabet, Q is a finite set of states, I Q is a set of initial states, F Q is a set of accepting states, and QQ is the transition relation. Let B (, Q, I, F, ) be a BA. A run of B on a word w 1, 2... starting in a state q0 Q is an infinite sequence q0, q1, ... such that qj1 j qj for all j 0. A run q0, q1, ... is accepting if q0 I and qi F for infinitely many i 0. The accepted language of B is defined as L(B) def w there exists an accepting run for w in B . Checking language inclusion between two B uchi automata is PSPACE-complete 18 , though decidable. Although the computational complexity is large, several approaches for checking language inclusion and counterexample (diff witness) generation have been implemented and produce promising results in practice 2 .

contexts.name: Refinement checking method via transformation to Buchi automata and language inclusion
contexts.description: Transforms finite TSPAs to Buchi automata and uses automated language inclusion checking with RABIT to verify refinement and generate witnesses for non-refinement.
contexts.original_text: A transformation from finite TSPAs to Buchi automata. A proof showing the operational semantics of a finite TSPA and the language accepted by the Buchi automaton resulting from such a transformation coincide. The result that refinement checking and disproof generation in form of semantic difference witnesses for software architectures where components can be mapped to finite TSPAs can be reduced to language inclusion checking and counterexample generation for Buchi automata. An implementation based on MontiArcAutomaton and RABIT.

contexts.name: Butterfly Space
contexts.description: A method-level static call graph centered on a seed method, including methods that call the seed (upper wing) and methods called by the seed (lower wing), used to analyze architectural impacts on performance.
contexts.original_text: In this paper, we propose a new architectural modeling approach based on the static analysis of method calls, named Butterfly Space modeling, to help detect and diagnose performance issues. Each butterfly space is a method-level static call graph, where the vertices are a subset of methods from the entire system and the edges are the method calls that are statically extracted. It contains three key parts: 1) a seed method, which is the center of the space because of its relationship with other methods in the space; 2) the upper wing which contains all the methods that call the seed directly or transitively; and 3) the lower wing, which contains all the methods called by the seed directly or transitively.

contexts.name: Precision and Recall in Performance Analysis
contexts.description: Metrics to evaluate how effectively a Butterfly Space captures performance optimization opportunities: precision is the proportion of methods with performance fixes in the space; recall is the proportion of all performance-fixed methods captured by the space.
contexts.original_text: We propose to use two measurements, precision and recall borrowed from information retrieval field, to evaluate how effective it is to examine a particular Butterfly Space to capture performance optimization opportunities. The precision and recall of a Butterfly Space is defined as: Precision: it is the number of methods with performance fixes in a Butterfly Space divided by the total number of methods in this space. ... Recall: it is the number of methods with performance fixes in a Butterfly Space divided by the total number of methods with performance fixes in the system.

contexts.name: Architectural Root Detection Algorithm
contexts.description: An algorithm to identify minimal sets of design spaces that aggregate bug-prone files, adapted here to method-level Butterfly Spaces to study architectural connections among performance optimization methods.
contexts.original_text: Cai et. al developed an Architectural Root (ArchRoot) detection algorithm. ... The ArchRoot detection algorithm takes two inputs 1) the comprehensive set of design spaces, calculated by using each and every source file in the system as the leading file; and 2) a list of bug-prone files in a system. The output ... are called the architectural roots of bug-proneness ... This paper employs the ArchRoot detection algorithm to investigate how and to what extent methods with performance optimization opportunities are architecturally connected with each other. Therefore, we replace the two inputs to the ArchRoot detection algorithm by 1) a comprehensive set of Butterfly Spaces that are calculated by using each and every method as the seed; and 2) the ground truth list of methods undertaken performance optimization.

contexts.text: If the seed method of a Butterfly Space contains performance problems, how likely the other methods in the space also contain performance problems? In particular, how does this compare to butterfly spaces whose seeds are free of performance issues?
contexts.original_text: RQ1: If the seed method of a Butterfly Space contains performance problems, how likely the other methods in the space also contain performance problems? In particular, how does this compare to butterfly spaces whose seeds are free of performance issues? We assume that if the seed of a Butterfly Space contains performance problems, the other methods in the space are also likely to contain performance problems. The rationale is that the seed method calls or is called by all the other methods in the space, directly or transitively. Therefore, the performance of the seed impacts and is impacted by the other methods in the space. In comparison, if the seed of a Butterfly Space is free of performance problems, the rest of the space are less likely to contain performance improvement opportunities. To answer this question, we will examine the precision and recall of Butterfly Spaces whose seed contains performance problem, and compare these measurements with that of Butterfly Spaces whose seed does not contain any problems. If the precision and recall of the former is significantly higher than the latter, it implies that when developers are revising a method for improving performance, he she should also prioritize and examine the methods in its Butterfly Space to capture more optimization opportunities at the same time. We envision this heuristic will help improve the efficiency of performance optimization localization for developers.

contexts.text: What is the advantage of Butterfly Space modeling in identifying performance optimization opportunities compared to dynamic profiling?
contexts.original_text: RQ2: What is the advantage of Butterfly Space modeling in identifying performance optimization op- portunities compared to dynamic profiling? Dynamic profiling suffers from two intrinsic limitations in identi- fying performance optimization opportunities. First, it is expensive and sometimes impractical to generate a large amount of high quality test data to reveal performance problems. Second, dynamic profiling relies on identifying the hot spot methods whose dynamic metrics are higher than average methods. However, sometimes performance optimization happens in methods whose dynamic met- rics look average. To capture all possible performance optimization opportunities, dynamic profiling is close to random searching and thus is not applicable. This RQ investigates the potential advantages of using Butterfly Spaces compared to dynamic profiling approaches. We use the ArchRoot detection algorithm to identify a set of root Butterfly Spaces that aggregate methods undertaken performance optimization. We compare the accumulative precision and recall of the top root Butterfly Spaces with dynamic profiling in two hypothetical settings. First, suppose developers can only afford to review a limited number of methods whose dynamic metrics ranks in the top 30 in a project. We compare the accumulative precision and recall of the top few Butterfly Spaces containing comparable or smaller number of methods. If the precision and recall of Butterfly Spaces are higher, it implies that Butterfly Spaces have the potential to improve the efficiency of identifying performance improvement opportunities with comparable effort as dynamic profiling. Second, suppose developers aim at identifying all the methods that need performance optimization, the dynamic profiling becomes almost like random searching. We will investigate the number of root Butterfly Spaces that need to be examined to reach a cumulative recall of 100 . And we will compare the total number of methods included in these spaces, and the cumulative precision. If the precision is higher, while the number of methods is smaller than using dynamic profiling, it indicates that Butterfly Spaces have the potential to help comprehensively capture all the performance improvement opportunities with higher accuracy but less effort.

contexts.text: What typical architectural patterns are responsible for performance problems can be revealed when combining Butterfly Space with dynamic metrics?
contexts.original_text: RQ3: What typical architectural patterns are respon- sible for performance problems can be revealed when combining Butterfly Space with dynamic metrics? The goal of this RQ is to evaluate the potential of combining Butterfly Space with dynamic metrics to provide fundamen- tal and qualitative understanding of whether exist and what are the typical architectural patterns in the root Butterfly Spaces that are responsible for the performance problems. This will provide more in-depth insights for developers when using Butterfly Spaces to identify architecturally connected performance improvement opportunities with limited dynamic data or historical fixing information.

contexts.text: There is a lack of practical approaches to align software architecture with business goals in the automotive domain.
contexts.original_text: While the software architecture community has acknowledged the need to align business goals with architectural decisions, there is a lack of practical approaches to achieve this alignment.

contexts.name: Business Goals
contexts.description: Objectives that a business anticipates to accomplish in a defined period of time, classified into categories such as growth, financial objectives, responsibilities, market position, and quality management. They are a main source of architecturally significant requirements (ASRs).
contexts.original_text: Business Goals are objectives that a business anticipates to accomplish in a defined period time. Clements et al. classify business goals in ten categories being (i) maintaining growth and continuity of the business, (ii) meeting the company financial objectives, (iii) meeting personal objectives, (iv) meeting responsibility to employees, (v) meeting responsibility to society, (vi) meeting responsibility to country, (vii) meeting responsibility to shareholders, (viii) managing market position, (ix) improving business processes, and (x) managing quality and reputation of products. Well-known automotive business goals include, for instance, product evolution after-sale and increased OEM control over unknown concerns. Business goals are crucial when architecting software systems. Bass et al. identify business goals as the main source of ASRs, which are requirements that have a profound impact on the architecture of a software system.

contexts.name: Architectural Tactics
contexts.description: Design decisions affecting the achievement of a single quality attribute response, used to extend architectural patterns and make software architecture design more systematic.
contexts.original_text: Architectural tactics or simply tactics are design decisions affecting the achievement of QA responses. It is important to note that the focus of a tactic is on a single QA response hence there a tactic does not focus on trade-offs. Bass et al. consider tactics pivotal for three main reasons. Tactics give the architects insights into the properties of a fragment of software architecture. Tactics can be used for extending an existing architectural pattern. Finally, tactics provide a convenient way to make the design of software architectures more systematic.

contexts.text: Speed of adaptation to changing demand in factory automation is critical, but integrating and deploying updates during costly production stops is expensive. The challenge is to enable dynamic reconfiguration of distributed embedded applications during operation without stopping the system and while maintaining real-time constraints and system reactivity.
contexts.original_text: Speed of adaptation to changing demand is a critical success factor in factory automation. The key to speed is to enable agile development by independent engineer offices and equipment producers with industrial-grade microservice architectures. The expensive drawback is: While software components evolve over time, manufacturers have to integrate and deploy more and more updates during costly production stops. To avoid production stops as much as possible, we propose reconfiguration extensions to a real-time container architecture proposed earlier. The original container approach addresses both the functional and non- functional aspects of integrating embedded software components in late engineering phases. The extended approach allows modifications of the running distributed embedded application even during operation, while continuously ensuring reactivity of the system.

contexts.name: Real-time container architecture
contexts.description: An architecture that isolates embedded software components in containers, managed by agents on each node to configure and trigger computation, communication, and I/O at specific times, enabling integration and reconfiguration of distributed embedded applications with real-time constraints.
contexts.original_text: Consistency and quality of distributed embedded applications have been addressed for the static case (without dynamic updates) by the real-time container architecture described in 2 . First, the architecture isolates each embedded component in a container. Second, a real-time container agent (agent) on each node configures the containers and the distributed system appropriately and actively triggers computation, network communication and I O at specific points in time. This enables the isolated components to communicate with each other and with the equipment exactly as declared in their interfaces.

contexts.name: Cycle turnover as moment of tranquility
contexts.description: The cycle turnover in the real-time container architecture is a moment when no tasks are performed and no messages arrive or leave without active triggering, providing an opportunity for safe reconfiguration without blocking the system.
contexts.original_text: Regarding consistency we cannot use the common blocking approach to dynamic reconfiguration of distributed systems, because we want to keep up reactivity of the embedded system. Instead, our approach exploits the cyclic behavior of the real-time container architecture: The cycle turn-over is an opportunity for reconfiguration, as it is in fact a moment of tranquility (no task is performed and no message arrives leaves without active triggering by the agent).

contexts.name: Synchronous reconfiguration approach for distributed embedded applications
contexts.description: An extension to the real-time container architecture enabling deterministic concurrent reconfiguration of distributed embedded applications during operation without blocking, maintaining system reactivity and real-time constraints.
contexts.original_text: In this paper we extend the real-time container archi- tecture to enable deterministic concurrent reconfiguration of distributed embedded applications during operation. The major challenge we address is that some reconfiguration steps such as downloads or container initializations take a hardly predictable amount of time and resources, while other steps interfere with the application in a critical way and must be performed as a synchronized action of the distributed system. Therefore, the agents synchronously perform modifications using detailed instructions from a reconfiguration plan consisting of synchro- nization steps, background steps and real-time steps as needed for the application.

contexts.text: There is no dedicated architectural guidance on how to design and architect microservices in a service mesh environment, leading to uncertainty and difficulty in selecting design and technology options.
contexts.original_text: Unfortunately so far no dedicated architectural guidance exists on how to design and architect microservices in a service mesh environment apart from practitioner blogs, industry white papers, experience reports, system documentations, and similar informal literature (sometimes called gray literature). This includes that so far there is no guidance for users of service mesh technologies or even their implementors to select the right design and technology options based on their respective properties. Very often it is even difficult to understand what all the possible design options, their possible combination, and their impacts on relevant quality properties and other decision drivers are. As a result, there is substantial uncertainty in architecting microservices in a service mesh environment, which can only be addressed by gaining extensive personal experience or gathering the architectural knowledge from the diverse, often incomplete, and often inconsistent existing practitioner-oriented knowledge sources.

contexts.name: Service Mesh
contexts.description: An infrastructure for managing communication of containerized microservices using a network of lightweight proxies or sidecars forming a data plane managed by a control plane.
contexts.original_text: service meshes [15] have been introduced as an infrastructure for managing the communication of containerized microservices and perform many related tasks. For this, they usually use a network of lightweight proxies or sidecars that handle all the communication burden [12, 16]. As a result, the coupling between microservices and of microservices to the infrastructure services can get drastically reduced... The proxies or sidecars form a data plane that is typically managed by a control plane [22].

contexts.name: Qualitative Study of Service Mesh Practices
contexts.description: Performed a qualitative, in-depth study of 40 practitioner knowledge sources to systematically identify established practices and architectural design decisions in service mesh based architectures.
contexts.original_text: To alleviate these problems, we have performed a qualitative, in-depth study of 40 knowledge sources in which practitioners describe established practices. We have based our study on the model-based qualitative research method described in [26], which uses such documented practitioner sources as rather unbiased knowledge sources and systematically codes them using established coding and constant comparison methods [6] combined with precise software modeling, in order to develop a rigorously specified software model of established practices and their relations.

contexts.text: Investigate the feasibility of using architectural performance modelling and simulation tools to predict the performance of privacy-preserving data analytics systems.
contexts.original_text: Here we investigate the feasibility of using architectural performance modelling and simulation tools for predicting the performance of privacy- preserving data analytics systems.

contexts.text: Lack of accurate methods to predict performance characteristics of privacy-preserving data analytics systems before implementation.
contexts.original_text: So, accurate way to predict the performance of a privacy- preserving analytic system before implementing the system is important. But, to best of our knowledge, there is no any previous study on predicting performance characteristics of privacy-preserving data analytics systems accurately.

contexts.text: Need for a methodology to support design decisions by comparing potential architectural design alternatives for privacy-preserving data analytics systems.
contexts.original_text: Additionally, there are many subsidiary design decisions related to the selection of a system architecture, such as the number and arrangement of computing nodes, the computing power of each node, and cryptographic key length. So, a methodology for supporting design decisions by allowing to compare potential design decisions is also equally important when adapting privacy-preserving data analytics systems.

contexts.name: Privacy-preserving data analytics
contexts.description: Technology allowing multiple parties to perform joint data analytics without disclosing source data to each other or a trusted third-party, using cryptographic techniques such as Homomorphic Encryption, Secret Sharing, and Garbled Circuits.
contexts.original_text: Privacy-preserving data analytics is an emerging technology which allows analytics to be performed on data owned by multiple semi non-trusted parties without data being disclosed to either party or a trusted third-party. A number of privacy- preserving data analytics platforms and protocols have been introduced 1 , 2 , 3 based on a variety of cryptographic building blocks such as Homomorphic Encryption 4 , 5 , Secret Sharing 6 , and Garbled Circuits 7 .

contexts.name: Architectural performance modelling
contexts.description: Techniques to model software system structure and performance aspects to predict non-functional attributes such as latency, resource usage, cost, and throughput, using frameworks like Palladio Component Model and simulation or analytical solvers.
contexts.original_text: Performance modelling has been thoroughly studied and has been shown to be able to predict the performance of various types of software systems. Two main classes of performance models are: Analytical models: represent the performance aspects of a software system as input for analytical solvers. Some popular examples are Petri nets (PN) 11 , Queue- ing Networks (QN) 12 , Layered Queueing networks (LQN) 13 . Architectural models: capture the structure of the system and main factors that influence its performance. Palla- dio Component Model (PCM) 14 , and the Descartes Modelling Language 15 are example frameworks. Architecture models can be converted to analytical models to be solved using analytical model solver or can be directly simulated using an architectural model simulator for obtaining performance predictions. Simulations can be more time consuming than analytic solvers but provide more flexibility in modelling. Non-functional attributes such as latency, resource usage, cost and throughput related to the structure and behaviour of a software system can be incorporated within architectural models. The resulting models can be fed to simulation engines or analytical solvers to predict non-functional performance at different stages of the development life cycle 16 . Additionally, Architectural models allow the description of the system on a higher level of abstraction and natural connection of components can be modelled which is not possible with analytical models. In this study, we modelled architecture performance char- acteristics of systems using N1 Analytics with the Palladio workbench 14 . The selection of Palladio was due to its free availability, simulation support, familiar UML-like interface provided for model creation, and the flexibility for incor- porating extensions such as architectural optimisation 17 , 18 , new qualities 19 , and new kinds of systems 20 . Palladio modelling concepts are aligned with component-based development, supporting re-use of modelled components.

contexts.original_text: However, existing approaches are limited to analyzing the change propagation in software systems or business processes in isolation.

contexts.text: It is challenging to analyze change propagation between business processes and information systems due to their complex mutual dependencies.
contexts.original_text: Thus, the mutual dependencies make the analysis of the change propagation challenging.

contexts.text: Current methods do not adequately support automated change impact analysis considering both business processes and information systems together.
contexts.original_text: However, they either do not support estimating the change efforts as an activity list to implement a change request, or do not offer an automated change impact analysis.

contexts.text: Software architects lack methods to analyze the effects of informal knowledge about quality attributes (QAs) such as usability and security on software architecture design decisions, especially when these QAs cannot be quantified or analyzed with existing techniques.
contexts.original_text: Software architects often have implicit knowledge about such effects on QAs of different software components. However, this knowledge is often only informally available and cannot be used in automated analysis and decision processes. Moreover, QAs such as security or usability often lack applicable analysis techniques. In approaches for design time quality prediction such QAs often remain unconsidered due to missing quantification and analysis techniques, although they are often crucial for the success of a project. Due to the lack of possibilities for considering informal knowledge in systematic decision support approaches, important trade-off decisions between performance and other quality requirements cannot be analyzed sufficiently.

contexts.text: Existing design-time quality prediction approaches like Palladio and PerOpteryx are limited to quantified QAs and cannot analyze complex relationships between informal knowledge about QAs, leaving important effects unconsidered.
contexts.original_text: The Palladio [19] approach together with PerOpteryx [12] is one example for design-time quality prediction and decision support for component-based software architectures. With the help of Palladio software architects can evaluate their design decisions with the focus on QAs such as performance, reliability, and maintainability at design time. On the basis of Palladio’s analysis engine, PerOpteryx evaluates architecture candidates resulting in the Pareto-optimal solutions. However, the analysis is limited to quantified QAs such as performance. In our previous work [5], we have extended the PerOpteryx approach so that not-quantified QAs can be analyzed in a very simple manner. However, this extension and also other existing approaches, such as ArcheE [2], or ArcheOpteryx [1], can not analyze complex relationships between modeled knowledge such as the mutual effect between usability and security. Therefore, when using approaches that rely on quantified QAs to analyze the software architecture quality, informal knowledge remains unconsidered.

contexts.name: Palladio Component Model
contexts.description: An approach for defining software architectures focusing on performance quality attributes, using component models with service effect specifications and resource-demanding service effect specifications to enable performance simulation and analysis.
contexts.original_text: For our approach, we use two approaches namely Palladio and PerOpteryx for software quality analysis and optimization as a basis and extended it in order to consider interferences of not-quantified QAs in the design space optimization.2.1 Architecture Model: Palladio Component ModelPalladio is an approach for the definition of software architectures with focus on performance QAs [19]. Several parts of this introductory section are taken from [10].As our running example let us consider the Business Reporting System (BRS) model. The BRS allows users to retrieve statistical analysis of business processes. For this purpose, the system allows the user to generate graphical and online reports. The system is roughly based on a real system [22]. The architecture model specified by the software architect consists of nine software components deployed on four different hardware nodes. The software components contain cost annotations, while the hardware nodes are annotated with performance units (processing rates) and cost (fixed and variable cost for example in EUR) units.For each software component service, the component developers provide an abstract behavioral description called service effect specification (SEFF). SEFFs model the abstract control flow through a component service in terms of internal actions (i.e., resource demands accessing the underlying hardware) and external calls (i.e., accessing connected components). SEFFs are composed automatically to determine the system-wide behavior. Modeling each component behavior with separate SEFFs enables us to quickly exchange component specifications without the need to manually change system-wide behavior specifications (as required in e.g. UML sequence diagrams).For performance annotations, component developers can use the extended resource-demanding service effect specifications (RDSEFFs). Using RDSEFFs, developers specify resource demands for their components (e.g., in terms of CPU instructions to be executed).A software architect composes component specifications modeled by various component developers to create a system model. The performance simulation finally is performed by solving such a model analytically or simulation-based. In this paper, we use the transformation from PCM to Layered Queueing Networks [7].
